title: A Fuzzy Sphere Journey in Critical Phenomena
comment: Invited review. Submitted May 2025; revised September 2025; published March 2026
summary: This review discusses the recently proposed fuzzy sphere regularization for studying $2+1$D critical phenomena, particularly three-dimensional (3D) conformal field theory (CFT). The fuzzy sphere scheme not only offers remarkable efficiency in extracting extensive CFT data at low computational cost but also reveals unexpected connections among 3D CFT (critical phenomena), noncommutative geometry, and the quantum Hall effect. We introduce the fundamental ideas of fuzzy sphere regularization, emphasizing its role in demonstrating the state-operator correspondence of 3D CFTs on the $S^2 \times \mathbb{R}$ geometry. Additionally, we review key developments in this approach across various directions and outline potential future applications.

AI.tldr: The paper reviews the fuzzy sphere regularization method for studying 2+1D critical phenomena and 3D conformal field theory, highlighting its computational efficiency, its demonstration of state-operator correspondence on S² × ℝ geometry, and its connections to noncommutative geometry and the quantum Hall effect.
AI.motivation: To introduce and review the fuzzy sphere regularization as an efficient computational approach for extracting 3D CFT data and to reveal unexpected connections among 3D CFT, noncommutative geometry, and the quantum Hall effect.
AI.method: Fuzzy sphere regularization — a scheme that uses noncommutative geometry to regularize theories on S² × ℝ, enabling the state-operator correspondence for 3D CFTs at low computational cost.
AI.result: The fuzzy sphere scheme achieves remarkable efficiency in extracting extensive CFT data and demonstrates the state-operator correspondence of 3D CFTs on S² × ℝ geometry.
AI.conclusion: The fuzzy sphere regularization is a powerful and efficient tool for studying 3D critical phenomena, with potential future applications across multiple directions linking CFT, noncommutative geometry, and the quantum Hall effect.

title: First passage time for an underdamped harmonic oscillator and application to the power of an information engine
summary: The distribution of the first passage time $t_{fp}$ for the position $x$ to overcome a threshold $x_B$ is calculated in an underdamped harmonic oscillator. The proof combines several approaches based on the determination of the eigenvalues of the Kramers differential operator for the intermediate and long time regimes and on a Hamiltonian approximation for the short times. The theoretical predictions are in excellent agreement with the results of an experiment on an underdamped micro-cantilever. The knowledge of the $t_{fp}$ distribution opens the way to several applications, among them the precise estimation of the power of information engines, which we have also experimentally checked.

AI.tldr: This paper calculates the first passage time distribution for an underdamped harmonic oscillator using eigenvalue analysis and Hamiltonian approximation, validated by micro-cantilever experiments and applied to information engine power estimation.
AI.motivation: To derive the first passage time distribution for an underdamped harmonic oscillator, enabling applications such as precise power estimation of information engines.
AI.method: Combines eigenvalue determination of the Kramers differential operator (for intermediate and long time regimes) with a Hamiltonian approximation (for short times).
AI.result: Theoretical predictions show excellent agreement with experimental results from an underdamped micro-cantilever, and the distribution was successfully applied to experimentally estimate information engine power.
AI.conclusion: The derived first passage time distribution is accurate and practically useful, particularly for characterizing information engines.

title: First passage time distribution in underdamped harmonic oscillators
summary: We derive the distribution of the first passage time $t_{fp}$ for the position $x$ of an underdamped harmonic oscillator to overcome a threshold $x_B$. As the $t_{fp}$ distribution depends on the oscillator quality factor $Q$ different approaches are used. At very large quality factor ($Q\gg 100$) and intermediate and long $t_{fp}$ the proof is based on an energy diffusion model, whereas at medium quality factor ($Q\sim 10$) the proof is based on the study of the eigenvalues of the Kramers linear differential operator with absorbing boundary conditions. For all $Q$ and short $t_{fp}$ we use a Hamiltonian approximation. The theoretical predictions are in excellent agreement with direct numerical simulations of underdamped oscillator dynamics. Finally we show that the mean of the trajectories ending at $t_{fp}$ presents a particular shape driven by a specific noise pattern.

AI.tldr: The paper derives the first passage time distribution for an underdamped harmonic oscillator crossing a threshold, using different analytical approaches depending on the quality factor Q, and validates results with numerical simulations.
AI.motivation: To analytically derive the first passage time distribution of an underdamped harmonic oscillator overcoming a threshold, which depends on the oscillator's quality factor Q.
AI.method: Three approaches: (1) energy diffusion model for very large Q (≫100) at intermediate/long times; (2) eigenvalue analysis of the Kramers linear differential operator with absorbing boundary conditions for medium Q (~10); (3) Hamiltonian approximation for all Q at short times.
AI.result: Theoretical predictions match excellently with direct numerical simulations of underdamped oscillator dynamics. The mean trajectory shape at first passage time is governed by a specific noise pattern.
AI.conclusion: The first passage time distribution for an underdamped harmonic oscillator can be accurately described using distinct analytical methods tailored to the quality factor regime, with full numerical validation.

title: Sandpile Models on complex networks
summary: We investigate the sandpile model on complex networks by developing a branching-process framework that explicitly incorporates dissipation during avalanche propagation. Unlike classical branching descriptions, which assume conservative transport and locally tree-like independence, the present approach introduces grain-loss effects directly into the offspring distribution, yielding generalized generating functions for dissipative avalanche dynamics. In the dissipative regime, avalanche-size distributions acquire exponential cutoffs while preserving topology-dependent scaling behavior. Numerical simulations confirm the theoretical predictions on sparse random networks and reveal systematic deviations in highly structured topologies. In particular, by using Holme-Kim clustered scale-free networks, we show that increasing clustering continuously lowers the avalanche exponent and enhances the probability of large cascades, demonstrating that short cycles generate strong correlations that invalidate the classical independent-branch approx imation. Surprisingly, trees also exhibit substantial deviations from power-law because low edge density and the abundance of leaves constrain avalanche propagation. These results show that dissipation, clustering, and sparse connectivity fundamentally reshape avalanche size distribution of the sandpile model on networks and establish quantitative limits for branching-process descriptions of avalanche dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a branching-process framework incorporating dissipation for the sandpile model on complex networks, showing that dissipation causes exponential cutoffs while clustering lowers avalanche exponents and sparse trees deviate from power-law behavior, establishing limits for branching-process approximations in avalanche dynamics.
AI.motivation: Classical branching-process descriptions of the sandpile model assume conservative transport and locally tree-like independence, ignoring dissipation effects. This work aims to incorporate grain-loss effects directly into the offspring distribution to better capture realistic avalanche dynamics on complex networks.
AI.method: The authors develop generalized generating functions for dissipative avalanche dynamics by introducing grain-loss effects into the offspring distribution. They validate predictions via numerical simulations on sparse random networks and Holme-Kim clustered scale-free networks, systematically varying clustering and topology.
AI.result: Avalanche-size distributions acquire exponential cutoffs in the dissipative regime while preserving topology-dependent scaling. Clustering continuously lowers the avalanche exponent and increases large-cascade probability due to short-cycle correlations. Trees deviate substantially from power-law behavior due to low edge density and leaf abundance.
AI.conclusion: Dissipation, clustering, and sparse connectivity fundamentally reshape avalanche size distributions, establishing quantitative limits for branching-process descriptions of avalanche dynamics on networks.

title: Learning Effective Soliton Dynamics from Scattering Data
summary: The inverse scattering transform (IST) provides the standard theoretical framework for deriving soliton dynamics. Traditionally, such derivations have been of an analytical, rather than data-driven, nature. In this paper, we combine the conceptual framework of the IST with weak-form system identification methods to discover effective soliton dynamics directly from observed scattering data, without assuming prior knowledge of the scattering equations. Our method avoids parameterizing solitary waves via ad hoc curve-fitting by working in the scattering domain, yielding interpretable low-dimensional models that remain valid in perturbed and near-integrable regimes. We demonstrate the performance of the proposed approach on synthetic and experimental data governed by shallow-water equations of Korteweg--de Vries-type and recover models that are consistent with canonical IST theory.

AI.tldr: The paper combines inverse scattering transform (IST) framework with weak-form system identification to learn soliton dynamics directly from data, without prior knowledge of scattering equations, producing interpretable low-dimensional models valid even in perturbed regimes.
AI.motivation: Traditional soliton dynamics derivations via IST are purely analytical; the authors aim to develop a data-driven approach that discovers these dynamics directly from observed scattering data without assuming prior knowledge of the scattering equations.
AI.method: The method integrates the conceptual framework of IST with weak-form system identification techniques, working in the scattering domain rather than using ad hoc curve-fitting for solitary wave parameterization.
AI.result: The approach successfully recovers low-dimensional models consistent with canonical IST theory, demonstrated on both synthetic and experimental shallow-water Korteweg–de Vries-type data, and remains effective in perturbed and near-integrable regimes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed data-driven IST framework enables interpretable soliton model discovery from scattering data, extending applicability to non-ideal regimes where traditional analytical IST derivations may be infeasible.

title: Ising superconductivity and anomalous metallic states in a bulk crystal with artificial unidirectional stacking layers
comment: main text 19 pages (4 figures) and SI 15 pages (11 figures)
summary: The two-dimensional (2D) limit in macroscopic bulk crystals provides a powerful platform for exploring exotic quantum phases. Here, we report the synthesis of a Sr0.75ClNbS2 superconductor that achieves unidirectional, parallel AA stacking-a configuration never before realized in a bulk crystal. Unlike conventional intercalation, which merely expands the interlayer spacing, our approach employs a planar Sr-Cl network to enforce a complete stacking reorganization, driving all NbS2 layers from the native antiparallel AB stacking into a unidirectional, parallel AA arrangement. This stacking switch globally breaks inversion symmetry, transforming centrosymmetric 2H-NbS2 into a noncentrosymmetric bulk crystal with D3h point group symmetry. Crucially, this structural design reproduces, in three dimensions, the electronic environment of an isolated monolayer, thereby preventing cancellation of the local Ising fields. As a result, strong Ising spin-orbit coupling and spin-split bands persist throughout the bulk. Transport measurements reveal extreme superconducting anisotropy (γ ~ 77), an in-plane upper critical field (~ 10.65 T) that far exceeds the Pauli paramagnetic limit, and clean-limit superconductivity indicative of high crystalline quality. Moreover, magnetotransport uncovers a novel magnetic-field-induced anomalous metallic state characterized by finite dissipation yet a vanishing Hall response. Direct band-structure measurements corroborate the layer-decoupled, quasi-2D electronic nature of the system. This work establishes stacking-geometry engineering as a powerful strategy to artificially enforce a globally noncentrosymmetric, quasi-2D superconducting state in bulk crystals, paving the way for designing quantum materials with tunable crystalline symmetry and electronic band topology.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the synthesis of a Sr0.75ClNbS2 bulk superconductor with unidirectional parallel AA stacking, achieved via a planar Sr-Cl network. This forces all NbS2 layers into a noncentrosymmetric D3h arrangement that preserves monolayer-like Ising spin-orbit coupling in 3D. The material exhibits extreme superconducting anisotropy (γ~77), anomalously high upper critical fields exceeding the Pauli limit, and a novel field-induced anomalous metallic state with finite dissipation but vanishing Hall response.
AI.motivation: To realize a globally noncentrosymmetric, quasi-2D superconducting state in a bulk crystal by engineering stacking geometry, overcoming the intrinsic inversion symmetry of native AB-stacked layered materials and enabling persistent Ising spin-orbit coupling in three dimensions.
AI.method: Synthesis of Sr0.75ClNbS2 via a planar Sr-Cl network that enforces complete stacking reorganization from native antiparallel AB stacking to unidirectional parallel AA stacking, combined with transport measurements, magnetotransport, and direct band-structure characterization.
AI.result: Achieved extreme superconducting anisotropy (γ~77), in-plane upper critical field (~10.65 T) exceeding the Pauli paramagnetic limit, clean-limit superconductivity, and observation of a magnetic-field-induced anomalous metallic state with finite dissipation but vanishing Hall response.
AI.conclusion: Stacking-geometry engineering is a powerful strategy to artificially enforce globally noncentrosymmetric, quasi-2D superconducting states in bulk crystals, offering a new route for designing quantum materials with tunable crystalline symmetry and electronic band topology.

title: Identical-Particle Symmetry-Enabled Complete Coherent Control of Ultracold Atomic and Molecular Collisions
summary: We show that exchange symmetry in collisions of identical particles enables symmetry-protected coherent control of the total scattering cross section. For identical fermions, antisymmetrization enforces complete phase synchronization of the contributing scattering channels, yielding maximal control visibility. For identical bosons, synchronization persists but with reduced visibility due to additional exchange (satellite) contributions. Collisions of distinguishable particles lack this symmetry-imposed phase locking, leading to lower controllability and visibility. We elucidate these principles through coupled-channel quantum-scattering calculations for lithium-lithium collisions, comparing the $^{6}\mathrm{Li}$-$^{6}\mathrm{Li}$ (identical fermions), $^{7}\mathrm{Li}$-$^{7}\mathrm{Li}$ (identical bosons), and $^{6}\mathrm{Li}$-$^{7}\mathrm{Li}$ (distinguishable) systems. Furthermore, in the identical particle cases, symmetry-enforced synchronization enables full control over the parity of the final state at any collisional energy. This mechanism is broadly applicable to identical-particle collisions, including homonuclear molecules for which established approaches -- DC electric fields, or microwave shielding -- are ineffective or unavailable.

AI.tldr: Exchange symmetry in identical-particle collisions enables symmetry-protected coherent control of scattering cross sections, with fermions achieving maximal control visibility, bosons reduced visibility, and distinguishable particles lacking this phase locking. Demonstrated via Li-Li collision calculations.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that exchange symmetry in collisions of identical particles enables symmetry-protected coherent control of the total scattering cross section, which is not possible for distinguishable particles.
AI.method: Coupled-channel quantum-scattering calculations for lithium-lithium collisions comparing ⁶Li-⁶Li (identical fermions), ⁷Li-⁷Li (identical bosons), and ⁶Li-⁷Li (distinguishable) systems.
AI.result: Identical fermions achieve maximal control visibility due to complete phase synchronization from antisymmetrization. Identical bosons show synchronization but reduced visibility due to exchange satellite contributions. Distinguishable particles lack symmetry-imposed phase locking, yielding lower controllability. For identical particles, symmetry-enforced synchronization enables full control over final-state parity at any collisional energy.
AI.conclusion: This symmetry-protected mechanism is broadly applicable to identical-particle collisions, including homonuclear molecules where DC electric fields or microwave shielding are ineffective or unavailable.

title: Fabrication of high-quality topological insulator nanodevices from bulk-insulating air-sensitive Sb-Bi$_2$Se$_3$
comment: 20 pages total; 9 pages main text with 5 figures and 11 pages of supplement with 8 figures
summary: High-quality topological insulator (TI) materials are essential for the realization and detection of Majorana bound states (MBSs) in TI-superconductor hybrid platforms. Widely used compensated TIs exhibit substantial disorder and charge inhomogeneity, which may be detrimental for Majorana devices. In this regard, Sb-substituted Bi$_2$Se$_3$ (SBS) is promising, because it is non-compensated and yet achieves very low bulk carrier density. We systematically investigate the impact of thermal processing during microfabrication on the transport properties of SBS. We developed a room-temperature fabrication protocol that preserves the low carrier density of exfoliated SBS upon fabrication of Hall bar and nanowire devices as evidenced from the observation of quantum interference oscillations in nanowires, a large gate tunability, and clear signatures of weak antilocalization (WAL).

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how thermal processing during microfabrication affects Sb-substituted Bi₂Se₃ (SBS), a non-compensated topological insulator with low bulk carrier density. A room-temperature fabrication protocol is developed that preserves low carrier density in exfoliated SBS devices, evidenced by quantum interference oscillations, large gate tunability, and weak antilocalization signatures.
AI.motivation: High-quality topological insulator (TI) materials are essential for realizing and detecting Majorana bound states (MBSs) in TI-superconductor hybrid platforms. Widely used compensated TIs suffer from disorder and charge inhomogeneity detrimental to Majorana devices. Non-compensated Sb-substituted Bi₂Se₃ (SBS) is promising but its response to thermal processing during microfabrication needs investigation.
AI.method: The authors systematically investigate the impact of thermal processing during microfabrication on SBS transport properties, and develop a room-temperature fabrication protocol to preserve low carrier density in exfoliated SBS Hall bar and nanowire devices.
AI.result: The room-temperature fabrication protocol preserves low carrier density, evidenced by quantum interference oscillations in nanowires, large gate tunability, and clear signatures of weak antilocalization (WAL).
AI.conclusion: The developed room-temperature fabrication protocol effectively preserves the low carrier density and high quality of SBS, making it a promising material platform for Majorana devices.

title: From Dirac Cones to Semions: An Exact Finite-Size Theory of Parity-Anomaly Transport in Chiral Spin Liquids
summary: Chiral spin liquids carry a hidden bookkeeping problem: the integer Chern number of their fractionalized spinons, the level of the emergent Chern--Simons gauge field, and the fractional spin response actually measured in experiment or simulation are related but distinct quantities, and the literature routinely conflates them. Here we resolve this by deriving the exact parity-odd determinant of a gapped Dirac cone on a spatial cylinder, resummed to all orders in the compact holonomy rather than truncated at leading order. The result proves that finite-circumference corrections to the topological response are strictly exponential, with no universal $1/L$ term, and fixes the precise map from microscopic spinon Chern number to physical spin Hall conductance. We validate this chain of reasoning on the kagome lattice at three independent levels: an exact parton band-structure calculation ($C=-1$, converging exponentially over cylinders four to twelve sites wide), and an interacting density-matrix renormalization group flux pump ($ν_s=-0.500\pm0.011$) that agrees with the analytic prediction without any adjustable parameter. Together, these results turn a one-loop anomaly calculation into a quantitatively verified bridge between microscopic topology and observable fractional response.

AI.tldr: The authors resolve a long-standing confusion in chiral spin liquids by showing that finite-circumference corrections to the topological response are strictly exponential (no universal 1/L term) and establishing the precise mapping between spinon Chern number and physical spin Hall conductance, validated via exact parton calculations and DMRG flux pump on the kagome lattice.
AI.motivation: The literature routinely conflates three related but distinct quantities—the integer Chern number of fractionalized spinons, the level of the emergent Chern-Simons gauge field, and the fractional spin response—creating a hidden bookkeeping problem that this work aims to resolve.
AI.method: Derives the exact parity-odd determinant of a gapped Dirac cone on a spatial cylinder, resummed to all orders in the compact holonomy; validates via exact parton band-structure calculations on cylinders 4–12 sites wide and interacting DMRG flux pump on the kagome lattice.
AI.result: Finite-circumference corrections to the topological response are strictly exponential with no universal 1/L term; the predicted spin Hall conductance (ν_s = -0.500 ± 0.011) agrees with the analytic prediction without any adjustable parameters.
AI.conclusion: The work turns a one-loop anomaly calculation into a quantitatively verified bridge between microscopic topology and observable fractional response, establishing a precise map from spinon Chern number to physical spin Hall conductance.

title: Transiently Driven Reflectionless Resonant Microwave Plasmas via Virtual Critical Coupling
comment: 7 Pages, 7 Figures, Submitted to IEEE TMTT
summary: Microwave plasma sources play a critical role in scientific research and a wide range of industrial, biomedical, and space applications. Resonant microwave structures have recently enabled highly energy-efficient plasma generation by concentrating electromagnetic energy within compact volumes. However, once plasma is ignited, the formation of a conductive region at the resonator's electric-field hotspot significantly perturbs the resonant impedance, resulting in severe impedance mismatch, increased reflection, and reduced power-transfer efficiency. This limitation arises because conventional resonant operation relies on critical coupling, in which the input coupling simultaneously provides impedance matching and perturbs the resonator. This paper overcomes this fundamental limitation by operating the resonator in an over-coupled regime and achieving dynamic impedance matching through temporally modulated excitation. Specifically, an exponentially growing incident waveform is used to emulate the critical coupling condition without physically modifying the resonator, a concept known as virtual critical coupling. The proposed approach enables the resonator to store up to four times as much electromagnetic energy as a conventionally critically coupled resonator. Experimental results demonstrate ultra-efficient resonant microwave plasma generation with multi-fold reductions in ignition energy consumption and enhanced dynamic control over plasma dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper overcomes impedance mismatch in resonant microwave plasma sources by operating in an over-coupled regime with temporally modulated excitation (virtual critical coupling), enabling up to 4x energy storage, reduced ignition energy, and enhanced plasma control.
AI.motivation: Conventional resonant microwave plasma generation suffers from impedance mismatch after plasma ignition due to conductive region formation at the resonator's hotspot, which reduces power-transfer efficiency. This limitation stems from critical coupling where input coupling simultaneously provides impedance matching and perturbs the resonator.
AI.method: Operate the resonator in an over-coupled regime with dynamic impedance matching via temporally modulated excitation, using an exponentially growing incident waveform to emulate critical coupling without physically modifying the resonator (virtual critical coupling).
AI.result: Up to 4x electromagnetic energy storage compared to conventional critically coupled resonators; multi-fold reductions in ignition energy consumption; enhanced dynamic control over plasma dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Virtual critical coupling via over-coupled operation and temporally modulated excitation is an effective approach to overcome the fundamental impedance mismatch limitation in resonant microwave plasma sources, achieving ultra-efficient plasma generation.

title: On the limits of the energetic coupling between field dislocation mechanics and phase field crystal
summary: This paper investigates the energetic coupling between Field Dislocation Mechanics (FDM) and the Phase Field Crystal (PFC) model proposed in Phys. Rev. B 102, 064109, 2020. While FDM correctly solves the initial boundary value problem of a continuum body with dislocation fields, PFC captures the underlying crystallographic structure. The coupling, which penalizes the $L^2$ distance between elastic distortion from FDM and configurational distortion from PFC in the $L^2$ sense, had been proposed to reconcile dislocation mechanics with crystallography in a single continuum framework. Variational analysis reveals that the coupling term acts as a divergence-driven forcing in the phase-field evolution that matches only the compatible (curl-free) parts of the distortion fields. Consequently, its contributions are insensitive to the incompatible (divergence-free) elastic distortion carrying all the information on dislocation topology. Furthermore, the nature of the configurational distortion causes mechanical boundary conditions to be transmitted diffusively from FDM to PFC rather than elastically. Numerical simulations demonstrate that this coupling cannot prevent the unnatural core spreading in FDM. Finally, it is shown that even in the most general case, an energetic coupling suffers from the same drawbacks, which limits its ability to integrate dislocation mechanics with crystallography.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the FDM-PFC coupling model and finds it ineffective because the coupling term only matches compatible (curl-free) distortion components, is insensitive to incompatible (divergence-free) elastic distortion containing dislocation topology, causes diffusive rather than elastic transmission of mechanical boundary conditions, and fails to prevent unnatural core spreading in FDM.
AI.motivation: To reconcile dislocation mechanics (FDM) with crystallography (PFC) in a unified continuum framework by energetically coupling the two models.
AI.method: Variational analysis of the energetic coupling term that penalizes the L² distance between elastic distortion from FDM and configurational distortion from PFC.
AI.result: The coupling term only captures compatible (curl-free) parts of distortion fields, is insensitive to incompatible (divergence-free) elastic distortion carrying dislocation topology information, transmits mechanical boundary conditions diffusively rather than elastically, and cannot prevent unnatural core spreading in FDM.
AI.conclusion: Even in the most general case, energetic coupling suffers from fundamental drawbacks that limit its ability to integrate dislocation mechanics with crystallography.

title: Complex dynamics in the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick game
comment: 24 pages, 13 figures in the main paper + 2 in appendix
summary: We study the outcome of adaptive learning of a large number of players engaging in sets of two-strategy two-player games. We are interested in typical games, and generate the payoff matrices at random at the beginning. The payoff matrices then remain fixed during the learning process. This provides a game theoretic foundation for the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) game, recently introduced by Garnier-Brun, Benzaquen and Bouchaud. The original model by these authors is a special case, with no bias towards any strategy. We here determine stability of learning for SK games with general random bias, and find that the nature of the stable state is affected by random fields. We also introduce a grand-canonical version of the SK game, in which players can choose to abstain. We determine the stability of learning for this game. Our analysis confirms that complex situations involving many players are frequently unlearnable, even if each player only chooses between two different actions. The rate with which players lose memory of past payoffs and the competitiveness of the game emerge as key parameters determining whether learning converges to a unique fixed point, whether there are many fixed points, or if the dynamics remains persistently volatile.

AI.tldr: The paper studies adaptive learning in large populations playing random two-strategy games (SK games), analyzing stability under general random bias and introducing a grand-canonical version with abstention options. Key parameters—memory loss rate and game competitiveness—determine whether learning converges to a unique/multiple fixed points or remains volatile.
AI.motivation: To provide a game-theoretic foundation for the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) game by analyzing adaptive learning outcomes in large populations playing random two-strategy games, extending previous work beyond the zero-bias special case.
AI.method: Random payoff matrices are generated at the start and remain fixed. Stability of adaptive learning is analyzed for SK games with general random bias, and a grand-canonical version allowing abstention is introduced and analyzed.
AI.result: Random fields (general bias) affect the nature of stable states. Complex multi-player situations are frequently unlearnable even with binary actions. The memory loss rate and game competitiveness are key parameters determining convergence to a unique fixed point, multiple fixed points, or persistent volatility.
AI.conclusion: The stability of learning in large-scale random games is governed by memory loss rate and competitiveness, with many systems being fundamentally unlearnable despite simple action spaces.

title: Enerzyme: A Framework for Efficient Training of Reactive Neural Network Potentials for Enzyme Catalysis with Application to Methyltransferases
summary: Quantum mechanical (QM) cluster models provide an effective framework for mechanistic studies of enzymatic reactions but remain computationally demanding. Neural network potentials (NNPs) offer a promising route to reduce this cost, but enzymes present challenges beyond small molecules, including large system sizes, implicit-solvent environments, substantial polarization, and charge transfer. Here, we present an integrated software framework for efficient NNP training for mechanistic studies of enzymes, demonstrated on QM cluster models of S-adenosyl-L-methionine-dependent methyltransferases (MTases). Our Enerzyme code introduces modular electrostatics-aware NNP architectures and combines automated QM-cluster construction with reactive dataset generation. The Enerzymette subpackage automates reaction pathway exploration at both NNP and DFT levels. We show that iterative flexible scans and nudged elastic band calculations impose stricter requirements on NNPs than conventional dataset metrics. Nevertheless, NNPs trained on fewer than 1,000 system-specific datapoints reproduce reaction energetics and transition-state structures for MTase clusters containing up to 545 atoms with near-chemical accuracy. Direct supervision of atomic charges and consistent dielectric screening substantially improve simulation stability and accuracy, while multitask-learned atomic charges capture charge transfer and polarization trends and provide chemically meaningful descriptors of reactivity. Finally, transferability across chemically diverse catechol O-methyltransferase substrates indicates that NNPs learn generalizable reactivity patterns as training data expand across multiple enzymes. Together, these results establish a foundation for accelerating enzyme mechanistic studies and guide future NNP development for biomolecular reactivity.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Enerzyme, an integrated software framework for training neural network potentials (NNPs) on quantum mechanical cluster models of enzymes. Applied to methyltransferases with up to 545 atoms, NNPs trained on fewer than 1,000 datapoints achieve near-chemical accuracy for reaction energetics and transition states. Key innovations include modular electrostatics-aware architectures, automated QM-cluster construction, direct supervision of atomic charges, consistent dielectric screening, and multitask-learned charges that capture polarization and charge transfer. Transferability across diverse catechol O-methyltransferase substrates shows NNPs learn generalizable reactivity patterns.
AI.motivation: QM cluster models are effective for enzymatic reaction studies but computationally demanding. NNPs could reduce this cost, but enzymes present challenges beyond small molecules—large system sizes, implicit-solvent environments, substantial polarization, and charge transfer—that existing NNP approaches do not adequately address.
AI.method: The Enerzyme framework integrates modular electrostatics-aware NNP architectures, automated QM-cluster construction, and reactive dataset generation. The Enerzymette subpackage automates reaction pathway exploration at NNP and DFT levels. Training uses iterative flexible scans and nudged elastic band calculations with fewer than 1,000 system-specific datapoints. Atomic charges are directly supervised via multitask learning, and dielectric screening is consistently applied.
AI.result: NNPs trained on fewer than 1,000 datapoints reproduce reaction energetics and transition-state structures for MTase clusters up to 545 atoms with near-chemical accuracy. Direct supervision of atomic charges and consistent dielectric screening substantially improve simulation stability and accuracy. Multitask-learned atomic charges capture charge transfer and polarization trends, providing chemically meaningful reactivity descriptors. Transferability across diverse COMT substrates demonstrates learning of generalizable reactivity patterns.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a foundation for accelerating enzyme mechanistic studies and provide guidance for future NNP development for biomolecular reactivity.

title: Path-Measure Dynamics of Attention-Driven World Models: A Nonlocal Onsager--Machlup Approach
summary: Attention enables a world model to condition on its entire history, providing long-term memory that facilitates long-range predictions. While the local Onsager--Machlup theory in our companion paper assumes a temporally local predictive action, we investigate the conditions under which this locality holds. We derive the predictive path measure for latent dynamics that become non-Markovian due to attention-induced memory, demonstrating that this measure is the projection of a hidden linear Markov augmentation. Eliminating the auxiliary field results in a nonlocal Onsager--Machlup action, where memory manifests as a nonlocal quadratic form rather than a force. These kernels are completely monotone and exactly match a hidden Markov embedding with a finite relaxation spectrum; otherwise, the dynamics remain fundamentally nonlocal. By expanding the action in terms of the scale-separation parameter $ε=τ_{\text{mem}}/τ_{\text{dyn}}$, we show that the leading order recovers the local action of the companion paper, establishing locality as the short-memory limit of a nonlocal theory. We verify the reversible sector of this expansion term by term against an exactly solvable vector linear model.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that attention-induced memory in world models leads to non-Markovian latent dynamics described by a nonlocal Onsager-Machlup action, which becomes local only in the short-memory limit (small τ_mem/τ_dyn). The nonlocal action matches a hidden Markov embedding with a finite relaxation spectrum, and the local limit recovers the companion paper's theory.
AI.motivation: To investigate when the temporally local predictive action assumed in the companion paper holds, given that attention provides long-term memory that can break Markovian locality.
AI.method: Derives the predictive path measure for latent dynamics with attention-induced memory, showing it as a projection of a hidden linear Markov augmentation. Expands the action via scale-separation parameter ε=τ_mem/τ_dyn and verifies against an exactly solvable vector linear model.
AI.result: The nonlocal Onsager-Machlup action has memory as a completely monotone nonlocal quadratic form. The leading-order expansion recovers the local action of the companion paper, establishing locality as the short-memory limit.
AI.conclusion: Locality of predictive action is valid only in the short-memory regime; otherwise, attention-induced memory yields fundamentally nonlocal dynamics, though they can be embedded in a finite-relaxation-spectrum hidden Markov model.

title: Verification and Performance Assessment of NuDEAL, a GPU-Accelerated Deterministic Transport Framework on Unstructured Meshes
comment: 39 pages, 14 tables, 15 figures. Author's original manuscript of an article published in Nuclear Science and Engineering. The final published version is available at https://doi.org/10.1080/00295639.2026.2652773
summary: High-fidelity neutronic analyses of advanced reactors require deterministic transport solvers capable of handling complex unstructured geometries while maintaining computational efficiency. This work presents the development and verification of three GPU-accelerated deterministic solvers implemented within a unified framework, Neutronics using Deterministic Finite Element Algorithm (NuDEAL): the planar Method of Characteristics coupled with the Hybrid Finite Element Method (MOC/HFEM), the Discontinuous Galerkin Method of Characteristics (DGMOC), and the Discontinuous Finite Element discrete ordinate method (DFEM-SN). These solvers provide complementary capabilities for consistently solving the multigroup transport equation and can be selectively employed to balance accuracy, computational cost, and memory requirements for a given problem. All methods emphasize efficient GPU execution by leveraging memory alignment, compressed-flux storage, and sequential azimuthal sweeps. The solvers are validated on the C5G7 benchmark and applied to advanced reactor problems, including the ABTR, Empire microreactor, and MSRE. DFEM-SN achieved the highest accuracy, with eigenvalue errors below 50 pcm, while MOC/HFEM and DGMOC provided superior efficiency, with single-GPU runtimes comparable to those of large CPU clusters. The results demonstrate that deterministic GPU solvers on unstructured meshes can deliver both accuracy and scalability, enabling practical whole-core simulations for heterogeneous advanced reactors. The unified NuDEAL framework establishes a foundation for future extensions toward transient and multiphysics analyses on large-scale GPU architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the development and verification of three GPU-accelerated deterministic transport solvers (MOC/HFEM, DGMOC, DFEM-SN) within the unified NuDEAL framework for high-fidelity neutronic analysis of advanced reactors. DFEM-SN achieves highest accuracy (eigenvalue errors <50 pcm), while MOC/HFEM and DGMOC offer superior efficiency with single-GPU performance comparable to large CPU clusters.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity neutronic analyses of advanced reactors require deterministic transport solvers capable of handling complex unstructured geometries while maintaining computational efficiency.
AI.method: Three GPU-accelerated solvers (MOC/HFEM, DGMOC, DFEM-SN) are implemented within the unified NuDEAL framework, leveraging memory alignment, compressed-flux storage, and sequential azimuthal sweeps for efficient GPU execution.
AI.result: DFEM-SN achieved eigenvalue errors below 50 pcm; MOC/HFEM and DGMOC achieved single-GPU runtimes comparable to large CPU clusters. Solvers validated on C5G7 benchmark and applied to ABTR, Empire microreactor, and MSRE.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic GPU solvers on unstructured meshes deliver both accuracy and scalability for heterogeneous advanced reactors. The NuDEAL framework provides a foundation for future transient and multiphysics analyses on large-scale GPU architectures.

title: Fermiology and spin polarization of topological surface states in PtBi$_2$
summary: Layered PtBi$_2$ is a candidate for topological superconductivity arising in Fermi-arc surface states. Using spin- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, we demonstrate that the Fermi arcs in PtBi$_2$ are singly degenerate and spin-polarized, which establishes their nontrivial topology and constitutes a necessary condition for topological superconductivity. We further uncover a pronounced surface-termination dependence of the Fermi-arc dispersion, yielding either nearly flat or approximately linear bands in agreement with first-principles calculations. Together, the observed spin polarization and termination-dependent bandwidth of the Fermi-arc surface states identify key ingredients underlying the potential emergence of topological superconductivity in PtBi$_2$.

AI.tldr: Spin-polarized, singly degenerate Fermi-arc surface states in PtBi₂ are confirmed via spin- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, revealing termination-dependent band dispersion (flat vs. linear) and establishing necessary conditions for topological superconductivity.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether PtBi₂ hosts nontrivial topological surface states (Fermi arcs) that are spin-polarized and singly degenerate, which are prerequisite conditions for topological superconductivity in this material.
AI.method: Spin- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (spin-ARPES) combined with first-principles calculations to probe the electronic structure, spin polarization, and surface-termination dependence of Fermi-arc states in layered PtBi₂.
AI.result: Fermi arcs in PtBi₂ are singly degenerate and spin-polarized, confirming nontrivial topology. A strong surface-termination dependence is observed: one termination yields nearly flat bands while the other gives approximately linear bands, consistent with DFT calculations.
AI.conclusion: The observed spin polarization and termination-dependent bandwidth of the Fermi arcs identify key electronic structure ingredients necessary for potential topological superconductivity in PtBi₂.

title: Microwave shielding of ultracold polar molecules on the transition $\boldsymbol{n=1 \rightarrow 2}$
summary: We show that microwave shielding on the rotational transition $n=1\rightarrow 2$ can be effective in preventing destructive collisions between ultracold polar molecules. It is slightly less efficient than shielding on the transition $0\rightarrow 1$, but has some important advantages. In particular, it does not produce 2-molecule bound states under the conditions needed for shielding, so it will not enhance 3-body recombination. It thus obviates the need for double-field microwave shielding using a second field of different polarization.

AI.tldr: Microwave shielding on the rotational transition n=1→2 prevents destructive collisions in ultracold polar molecules, is slightly less efficient than 0→1 shielding but avoids bound states that enhance 3-body recombination, eliminating the need for double-field microwave shielding.
AI.motivation: To find a method to prevent destructive collisions between ultracold polar molecules without creating bound states that enhance 3-body recombination, which is a problem with the 0→1 shielding approach.
AI.method: Investigating microwave shielding on the rotational transition n=1→2 as an alternative to the 0→1 transition.
AI.result: Microwave shielding on the 1→2 transition is slightly less efficient than 0→1 shielding but does not produce 2-molecule bound states under shielding conditions, thus not enhancing 3-body recombination.
AI.conclusion: The 1→2 microwave shielding approach obviates the need for double-field microwave shielding using a second field of different polarization, offering a simpler and more effective solution for preventing destructive collisions.

title: Resonant cooling of nuclear spins by optically-oriented holes in MAPbI$_3$ perovskite crystals
summary: Resonant cooling of nuclear spins by photogenerated spin-oriented holes is demonstrated for MAPbI$_3$ perovskite crystals. It is evidenced by Hanle-effect measurements under helicity-modulated excitation with variable frequency. The resonance position in magnetic field shifts toward higher fields with increasing modulation frequency. The invariance of the Hanle curve upon in-plane sample rotation is consistent with the involvement of $^{207}$Pb nuclei with spin $I = 1/2$, which do not exhibit quadrupolar splitting. The shape of the resonance feature in the Hanle curve reveals that the nuclear spins are cooled by carriers with a negative $g$-factor, consistent with holes. The resonance fields associated with the modulation frequencies exceed the half-width of the weakly localized hole contribution to the Hanle curve, indicating that strongly localized holes are the primary carriers responsible for the nuclear spin cooling.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates resonant cooling of nuclear spins by photogenerated spin-oriented holes in MAPbI₃ perovskite crystals, measured via Hanle-effect with helicity-modulated excitation. The resonance shifts to higher magnetic fields with increasing modulation frequency, and the data indicate that strongly localized holes with negative g-factor are responsible for cooling ²⁰⁷Pb nuclei (spin I=1/2).
AI.motivation: To demonstrate and characterize resonant nuclear spin cooling by spin-oriented holes in MAPbI₃ perovskite crystals, and to identify the specific nuclear species and carrier type involved in the process.
AI.method: Hanle-effect measurements under helicity-modulated excitation with variable modulation frequency; analysis of resonance position shifts in magnetic field; in-plane sample rotation studies to probe nuclear species.
AI.result: The resonance field shifts to higher fields with increasing modulation frequency; the Hanle curve is invariant under in-plane rotation, consistent with ²⁰⁷Pb nuclei (I=1/2, no quadrupolar splitting); the resonance feature shape indicates cooling by carriers with negative g-factor (holes); resonance fields exceed the half-width of weakly localized holes, pointing to strongly localized holes as the primary agents.
AI.conclusion: Resonant nuclear spin cooling via strongly localized holes with negative g-factor is achieved in MAPbI₃, involving ²⁰⁷Pb nuclei without quadrupolar effects.

title: Quantum Tunneling-induced Hybridization and Coherent Dynamics of Jackiw-Rebbi Zero Modes in a Modified Su-Schrieffer-Heeger Chain
summary: We investigate analytically and numerically the tunneling-induced hybridization and coherent dynamics of Jackiw-Rebbi (JR) zero modes in a modified Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model. Unlike the conventional SSH model, this modified system possess two bulk gap closing points, namely, the quadratic-type gap closing point at $k=0$ and the Dirac-type gap closing point at $k=\pmπ/4a$. While the quadratic point does not support a topological domain wall due to the absence of mass inversion, the low-energy Dirac theory around $k=\pmπ/4a$ predicts an effective mass that changes sign at two spatially separated interfaces under a kink profile, generating a pair of JR bound states localized at those interfaces. We show that finite overlap between the JR zero modes lifts the zero-energy degeneracy through quantum tunneling, producing symmetric-antisymmetric hybridized states analogous to a quantum mechanical double-well system. An effective two-level description reveals coherent oscillations of the occupation probability between the two JR modes, accompanied by periodic transfer of sublattice polarization between the (A,C) and (B,D) sectors. The oscillation period is governed by the hybridization gap, providing a tunable route for controlling topological bound states. Our results establish a unified framework connecting JR zero modes, quantum tunneling, and coherent dynamics in modified SSH systems, offering a promising platform for controllable topological quantum-state transfer in engineered lattice structures.

AI.tldr: The paper studies tunneling-induced hybridization and coherent dynamics of Jackiw-Rebbi zero modes in a modified SSH model with two bulk gap closing points ($k=0$ quadratic and $k=\pm\pi/4a$ Dirac). The Dirac point supports mass inversion at two interfaces under a kink profile, generating a pair of JR bound states. Tunneling between them lifts zero-energy degeneracy, producing hybridized states and coherent oscillations of occupation probability and sublattice polarization, with the oscillation period governed by the hybridization gap.
AI.motivation: To understand how quantum tunneling hybridizes Jackiw-Rebbi zero modes in a modified SSH model and to establish a controllable platform for topological quantum-state transfer.
AI.method: Analytical and numerical analysis of a modified SSH model with two gap-closing points (quadratic at $k=0$, Dirac at $k=\pm\pi/4a$), low-energy Dirac theory for effective mass kink profiles, and a two-level effective model describing tunneling-induced hybridization and coherent dynamics.
AI.result: Finite overlap between JR zero modes lifts degeneracy via quantum tunneling, creating symmetric-antisymmetric hybridized states (analogous to a double-well system). Coherent oscillations of occupation probability and sublattice polarization transfer occur between the two JR modes, with the oscillation period set by the hybridization gap.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a unified framework connecting JR zero modes, quantum tunneling, and coherent dynamics in modified SSH systems, offering a tunable platform for controllable topological quantum-state transfer in engineered lattices.

title: A 2048-spin bulk acoustic wave Ising machine for number partitioning and Sudoku
summary: Optical coherent Ising machines based on time-multiplexing have demonstrated significant progress in terms of connectivity and spin scalability. However, they are constrained by large physical footprints, high power consumption, poor thermal stability, and high cost. Here, we present a time-multiplexed Ising machine leveraging propagating wave packets in solid-state delay lines at microwave frequencies, enabling thermally stable, robust, low-power, tabletop, and affordable design. We use two serially connected 20.5 MHz, 707 μs bulk acoustic wave delay lines supporting 2,048 spins. Our design provides all-to-all connectivity with 15-bit coupling resolution and finds approximate MAX-CUT solutions in 341 ms, potentially scalable to sub-ms by using higher frequency delay lines. Additionally, we demonstrate solutions to number partitioning and Sudoku problems. Compared with state-of-the-art Coherent Ising machines, our machine exhibits four orders of magnitude higher thermal stability. Against the simulated bifurcation algorithm, our design achieves comparable results on the MAX-CUT problem, while outperforming it on the more complex number-partitioning and Sudoku problems.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a time-multiplexed Ising machine using microwave-frequency acoustic wave delay lines in solid-state, achieving thermally stable, low-power, tabletop operation with 2,048 spins, all-to-all connectivity, and faster solutions to MAX-CUT, number partitioning, and Sudoku problems compared to prior Coherent Ising machines and simulated bifurcation algorithms.
AI.motivation: Optical coherent Ising machines using time-multiplexing suffer from large physical footprints, high power consumption, poor thermal stability, and high cost, motivating the need for a more stable, compact, and affordable alternative.
AI.method: The authors implement a time-multiplexed Ising machine using two serially connected 20.5 MHz, 707 μs bulk acoustic wave delay lines at microwave frequencies, supporting 2,048 spins with all-to-all connectivity and 15-bit coupling resolution.
AI.result: The machine finds approximate MAX-CUT solutions in 341 ms (potentially scalable to sub-ms), exhibits four orders of magnitude higher thermal stability than state-of-the-art Coherent Ising machines, and achieves comparable MAX-CUT performance while outperforming simulated bifurcation on number-partitioning and Sudoku problems.
AI.conclusion: The proposed solid-state acoustic wave delay line Ising machine offers a thermally stable, robust, low-power, tabletop, and affordable platform for solving combinatorial optimization problems, with advantages over both optical Coherent Ising machines and simulated bifurcation algorithms.

title: Microscopic origins of inertial magnetization dynamics
comment: Main text: 4 pages 2 figures. Supplementary text: 9 pages 3 figures
summary: Ultrafast experiments have uncovered inertial magnetization dynamics in ferromagnets, but their microscopic origin remains elusive. Using a non-Markovian quantum master equation we show that inertial dynamics arise from coherent interactions with optical phonons in the lattice. The fast optical frequency explains the nutation observed on picosecond timescales and accounts for variations between experiments through substrate-dependent phonon damping. By establishing magnon{phonon coupling as the microscopic basis of inertial magnetization, our results open new pathways for tailoring ultrafast spin dynamics and controlling magnetic states at terahertz frequencies.

AI.tldr: The paper explains that inertial magnetization dynamics in ferromagnets arise from coherent magnon-phonon coupling, specifically with optical phonons, providing a microscopic basis for picosecond-timescale nutation observed in ultrafast experiments.
AI.motivation: The microscopic origin of inertial magnetization dynamics observed in ultrafast ferromagnet experiments remained elusive, motivating a theoretical explanation.
AI.method: A non-Markovian quantum master equation is used to model the coherent interaction between magnetization (magnons) and optical phonons in the lattice.
AI.result: Inertial dynamics arise from magnon-phonon coupling; the optical phonon frequency explains picosecond nutation timescales, and substrate-dependent phonon damping accounts for experimental variations.
AI.conclusion: Establishing magnon-phonon coupling as the microscopic basis opens pathways for tailoring ultrafast spin dynamics and controlling magnetic states at terahertz frequencies.

title: Vitriflow: calibrated amorphous structure ensembles from melt-quench simulation
summary: Melt--quench molecular dynamics is widely used to construct amorphous materials models, but the resulting ensemble is defined by choices that are often made implicitly: numerical settings, melt temperature, liquid-hold time, quench rate, system size, and post-generation screening. We introduce vitriflow, a computational materials methodology that turns these choices into an explicit decision chain. The framework couples numerical stability, descriptor-based protocol calibration, user-defined artefact screening, and statistical convergence of the generated analysis ensemble in a material-specific descriptor space. We demonstrate the approach for a-SiO$_2$, a-Si$_3$N$_4$, and a-Sm$_2$O$_3$, which respectively test tetrahedral network fidelity, MG2 $\rightarrow$ PBE $\rightarrow$ HSE06 DFT refinement of a heteropolar nitride, and amorphous/crystal discrimination in a mixed-coordination rare-earth oxide. vitriflow separates defect-free from oxygen-bridge-defective silica, quantifies DFT-refinement response in a common a-Si$_3$N$_4$ structural population, and removes recrystallised Sm$_2$O$_3$ structures without imposing fixed coordination. The result is a reproducible route for generating amorphous ensembles whose numerical settings, thermal protocol, screening actions, and statistical precision are selected from the materials question rather than assumed a priori.

AI.tldr: vitriflow is a computational methodology that turns implicit choices in melt-quench molecular dynamics (temperature, quench rate, system size, screening) into an explicit decision chain, demonstrated for a-SiO₂, a-Si₃N₄, and a-Sm₂O₃ to produce reproducible amorphous ensembles tailored to specific materials questions.
AI.motivation: Melt-quench MD simulations for amorphous materials rely on numerous implicit choices (temperature, hold time, quench rate, system size, screening) that lack standardization, leading to irreproducible and question-dependent ensembles.
AI.method: vitriflow couples numerical stability analysis, descriptor-based protocol calibration, user-defined artefact screening, and statistical convergence monitoring in a material-specific descriptor space to formalize the decision chain of melt-quench MD.
AI.result: The framework successfully separates defect-free from defective silica, quantifies DFT-refinement response across a shared structural population in a-Si₃N₄, and removes recrystallized structures in Sm₂O₃ without fixed coordination constraints.
AI.conclusion: vitriflow provides a reproducible, decision-chain-based route for generating amorphous ensembles where numerical settings, thermal protocols, screening actions, and statistical precision are selected based on the materials question rather than assumed by default.

title: Symmetry and Topology in Wavepacket Dynamics near Conical Intersections
summary: Whether topology directly shapes chemical dynamics remains an open question in theoretical chemistry. The issue arises because degeneracies of adiabatic electronic states can generate nontrivial topological structure, and such degeneracies are common in polyatomic molecules. Existing work has largely emphasized static characterizations and dynamical studies of low-energy, highly symmetric models. Here we develop a symmetry-based analysis of nonadiabatic dynamics in two-state conical-intersection models that is predictive without invoking topological invariants. We show that the nodal-line structures associated with dynamics near a conical intersection are robust in highly symmetric settings, but should not in general be expected to persist once the relevant symmetry is broken.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether topology directly shapes chemical dynamics near conical intersections, showing that symmetry-based analysis can predict nonadiabatic dynamics without topological invariants, and that nodal-line structures are robust only in highly symmetric settings but not under symmetry breaking.
AI.motivation: The open question of whether topology directly shapes chemical dynamics, given that degeneracies of adiabatic electronic states (common in polyatomic molecules) generate nontrivial topological structure, while existing work focuses on static characterizations and low-energy symmetric models.
AI.method: A symmetry-based analysis of nonadiabatic dynamics in two-state conical-intersection models that is predictive without invoking topological invariants.
AI.result: Nodal-line structures associated with dynamics near a conical intersection are robust in highly symmetric settings but should not generally be expected to persist when the relevant symmetry is broken.
AI.conclusion: Symmetry, rather than topology per se, is the key predictive framework for understanding nonadiabatic dynamics near conical intersections, and topological features are not robust under symmetry breaking.

title: Theory of collective learning in populations of adaptive agents
summary:
We investigate homogeneous populations of smart active agents that exchange information with their neighbors to perform a decentralized learning process aimed at achieving a prescribed macroscopic state. Such agents may, for example, represent simple microrobots. The exchanged information comprises tunable parameters governing the agent dynamics, referred to as the individual policy, together with an internal memory encoding previously visited states. This memory is used to evaluate a reward that quantifies the success of a policy to achieve the prescribed state. We extend the kinetic-theory description of collective learning in spatially homogeneous systems [Phys. Rev. Lett. 134, 248302 (2025)] and derive formal evolution equations for the distribution of policies across the population. A central outcome of our theory is the emergence of an effective reward function that fully determines the evolution of the policy distribution and encapsulates the microscopic details of the agents physical and memory dynamics. We obtain closed equations for the policy mean and variance which admit explicit time-dependent solutions under the assumption of Gaussian-distributed memories and polices.
  To illustrate the framework, we present a series of minimal microscopic models, considering both perfect and partial separation of physical, memory and policy exchange time scales, as well as models with one- and two-dimensional policies. The obtained theoretical results compare well with agent-based numerical simulations. The theory captures key aspects of collective learning, including the influence of population diversity and reward fluctuations on learning performance. Finally, we discuss potential applications to swarm robotics and machine learning, and highlight connections with classical models of biological evolution, including the Replicator equation and the Moran model.

AI.tldr: This paper extends kinetic theory to model decentralized collective learning in populations of smart agents (e.g., microrobots) that exchange policies and memory to achieve a prescribed macroscopic state. It derives evolution equations for policy distributions, reveals an effective reward function governing the dynamics, and obtains closed-form solutions under Gaussian assumptions. Theoretical results are validated via agent-based simulations and connected to evolutionary models like the Replicator equation and Moran model.
AI.motivation: To develop a theoretical framework for understanding how homogeneous populations of active agents (e.g., microrobots) can achieve a prescribed macroscopic state through decentralized information exchange and collective learning.
AI.method: Extends kinetic-theory description of collective learning in spatially homogeneous systems; derives formal evolution equations for the distribution of policies across the population; obtains closed equations for policy mean and variance under Gaussian-distributed memories and policies; validates with agent-based numerical simulations of minimal microscopic models.
AI.result: Derives an effective reward function that fully determines policy distribution evolution; obtains explicit time-dependent solutions for policy mean and variance; theoretical results match agent-based simulations; captures effects of population diversity and reward fluctuations on learning performance.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a unified theoretical description of collective learning, with connections to the Replicator equation and Moran model from biological evolution, and potential applications in swarm robotics and machine learning.

title: Predicting Novel Stable Materials for Experimental Synthesis
summary: Machine-learning-accelerated materials discovery has yielded large numbers of computationally stable compounds, yet many remain experimentally unrealized, underscoring a persistent gap between prediction and synthesis. Here, we introduce a hierarchical screening framework that combines PBE-based thermodynamic stability, efficient dynamical-stability screening enabled by universal machine-learning interatomic potentials, and SCAN-based thermodynamic refinement. Applying this protocol to the 894 stable materials previously reported in Sci. Data 9, 302 (2022), we first curate 603 unique structures, of which only 298 remain thermodynamically stable on the complete PBE phase diagrams, demonstrating the critical role of competing phases in stability assessment. Dynamical screening then identifies 166 materials stable under both harmonic-phonon and finite-temperature molecular dynamics criteria, and SCAN phase diagrams further narrow this set to 109. Finally, by combining decomposition enthalpy with chemical-space completeness, we prioritize 25 candidates as high-confidence targets for experimental synthesis. This work provides a practical protocol for translating stability predictions into experimentally actionable synthesis targets, closing a key gap in machine-learning-driven materials discovery.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical screening framework combining PBE stability, machine-learning-potential dynamical screening, and SCAN refinement reduces 894 computationally stable materials to 25 high-confidence experimental synthesis targets, closing the prediction-synthesis gap.
AI.motivation: Many computationally predicted stable materials remain experimentally unrealized, highlighting a persistent gap between computational prediction and experimental synthesis. The authors aim to bridge this gap by developing a practical protocol that translates stability predictions into actionable synthesis targets.
AI.method: A three-stage hierarchical screening pipeline: (1) PBE-based thermodynamic stability analysis with competing-phase assessment (894→298), (2) dynamical stability screening using universal ML interatomic potentials with both harmonic-phonon and finite-temperature MD criteria (298→166), (3) SCAN-based thermodynamic refinement (166→109), followed by decomposition enthalpy and chemical-space completeness prioritization (109→25).
AI.result: From 894 reported stable materials, only 603 unique structures were curated, 298 remained thermodynamically stable on complete PBE phase diagrams, 166 passed dynamical screening, 109 survived SCAN refinement, and 25 were prioritized as high-confidence experimental synthesis targets.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchical screening protocol effectively filters computationally predicted stable materials into a small set of experimentally actionable targets, demonstrating that competing phases, dynamical stability, and higher-accuracy thermodynamics are critical for reliable synthesis prediction, thereby closing the gap between ML-driven discovery and experimental realization.

title: Disorder-induced superconductivity in graphene
summary: Correlated phases of matter are typically investigated in crystalline systems, where disorder is considered to be detrimental. However, intriguing exceptions exist, such as superconductivity being enhanced in amorphous realizations of Al and Bi. Here, we demonstrate that superconductivity can even emerge entirely from disorder, using monolayer graphene as an example. In the clean limit, the semi-metallic nature of graphene requires prohibitively strong electronic interactions to achieve superconductivity. Despite the inherently random nature of disorder, we show that introducing low concentrations of vacancies or hydrogenation in graphene provides a large density of low-energy states that easily induce superconductivity. For conventional $s$-wave pairing, disorder induces a finite superconducting order parameter for arbitrarily weak attractive interactions. Rather than forming isolated superconducting puddles, global phase coherence is established through a finite superfluid weight of purely geometrical origin. Away from the chiral limit of vacancies, hydrogenation similarly yields a finite transition temperature and nonzero superfluid weight for weak interactions. For unconventional nearest-neighbor pairing, typically more disrupted by disorder, superconductivity exhibits quantum-critical-like behavior, yet phase coherence persists at low interaction strengths, with mixed $d$-wave symmetries. Our work demonstrates the robust emergence of macroscopic superconducting phase coherence engineered entirely from microscopic disorder.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that superconductivity can emerge purely from disorder in monolayer graphene, where introducing vacancies or hydrogenation creates low-energy states that induce superconductivity with global phase coherence, even for weak interactions.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that superconductivity can emerge entirely from disorder, challenging the conventional view that disorder is detrimental to correlated phases, using monolayer graphene as a platform where clean-limit superconductivity is prohibitively difficult.
AI.method: The authors introduce low concentrations of vacancies or hydrogenation in monolayer graphene and theoretically investigate the resulting electronic states, superconducting order parameter, superfluid weight, and phase coherence for both conventional s-wave and unconventional nearest-neighbor pairing channels.
AI.result: Disorder induces a finite superconducting order parameter for arbitrarily weak attractive interactions in s-wave pairing; global phase coherence arises from a purely geometrical superfluid weight; hydrogenation similarly yields finite Tc and superfluid weight; unconventional pairing shows quantum-critical-like behavior with mixed d-wave symmetries and persistent phase coherence at low interaction strengths.
AI.conclusion: Macroscopic superconducting phase coherence can be robustly engineered entirely from microscopic disorder, establishing disorder as a resource rather than a hindrance for inducing superconductivity.

title: Quantum Heat Under the Microscope: A Perspective on Cryogenic Scanning Thermal Microscopy
summary: Exploring thermal transport at cryogenic temperatures presents both significant challenges and valuable insights. By uncovering the thermal counterpart of well-known quantum phenomena, researchers investigated fascinating phenomena ranging from the violation of the Wiedemann-Franz law to the quantisation of phonons. One key frontier remains : no existing method can image local heat transport at the nanoscale under cryogenic conditions. In this Perspective, we review the current state state of the art of local heat transport characterisation techniques and highlight their limitations. As a motivation for the development of cryogenic Scanning Thermal Microscopy, we provide five case studies illustrating how this approach could deepen our understanding of exotic quantum phases and enable the emergence of transformative technologies.

AI.tldr: This Perspective reviews the limitations of current local heat transport characterization techniques at cryogenic temperatures and motivates the development of cryogenic Scanning Thermal Microscopy (SThM) through five case studies that could advance understanding of exotic quantum phases and enable transformative technologies.
AI.motivation: No existing method can image local heat transport at the nanoscale under cryogenic conditions, which hinders deeper understanding of quantum phenomena such as violation of the Wiedemann-Franz law and phonon quantization.
AI.method: The authors review the current state-of-the-art of local heat transport characterization techniques, identify their limitations, and propose five case studies to demonstrate how cryogenic Scanning Thermal Microscopy could address these gaps.
AI.result: Current techniques are inadequate for nanoscale local heat transport imaging at cryogenic temperatures; cryogenic SThM is presented as a promising approach to overcome these limitations.
AI.conclusion: Developing cryogenic Scanning Thermal Microscopy could deepen understanding of exotic quantum phases and enable transformative technologies by providing nanoscale thermal transport imaging capabilities previously unavailable.

title: Generalized quantum geometry formulated through interacting vertex correlations
summary: Quantum geometry characterizes the variation of electron wavefunctions in solids along a parameter space. Conventionally, crystal momentum is chosen as the parameter, since it couples to electromagnetic fields, offering an interpretation of quantum geometry in terms of dipole matrix elements, polarization fluctuations, and optical responses. However, Bloch momentum is not the only possible parameter space in which a wavefunction can evolve. In this work, we show that quantum geometry can be extended beyond the bare Bloch-band geometry to manifolds whose adiabatic parameters represent deformations of the ground state, including collective bosonic fluctuations, external fields, or structural distortions. We show that the generalized quantum geometric tensor is encoded by correlations of interacting vertices, conjugate to the deformation parameters. By way of illustration, we briefly discuss the application of these extended geometric concepts to manifolds generated by Hubbard-Stratonovich bosonic fields, or Jahn-Teller configurational spaces. The formulation presented here is framed by general manifolds, which extend quantum geometry to generic structural, collective, and interactive many-body systems.

AI.tldr: The paper extends quantum geometry beyond Bloch-band manifolds to include adiabatic parameters representing ground-state deformations such as collective bosonic fluctuations, external fields, or structural distortions, showing that the generalized quantum geometric tensor is encoded by correlations of interacting vertices.
AI.motivation: To generalize quantum geometry beyond the conventional Bloch momentum parameter space, enabling its application to many-body systems with collective, structural, and interactive degrees of freedom.
AI.method: The authors propose a generalized quantum geometric tensor framework where adiabatic parameters represent deformations of the ground state, and show it is encoded by correlations of interacting vertices conjugate to those deformation parameters.
AI.result: The formalism extends quantum geometry to general manifolds, including those generated by Hubbard-Stratonovich bosonic fields and Jahn-Teller configurational spaces.
AI.conclusion: Quantum geometry can be extended beyond bare Bloch-band geometry to generic structural, collective, and interactive many-body systems, where the geometric tensor is linked to correlation functions of interacting vertices.

title: Electrical transport in ultra-thin films: from Fuchs-Sondheimer to quantum-confinement
summary: Ultra-thin films are fundamental components of modern nanoelectronics, where reducing thickness to the few-nanometer scale leads to a dramatic increase in electrical resistivity. For decades, this behavior has been interpreted in terms of classical size effects, primarily surface scattering within the Fuchs--Sondheimer theory and grain-boundary scattering in the Mayadas--Shatzkes model. While these approaches successfully describe transport when the film thickness is comparable to the electronic mean free path, growing experimental evidence indicates that they become insufficient under extreme confinement. This review discusses the crossover from classical scattering to a quantum-confinement regime in which the electronic states available for transport are fundamentally restructured by finite size. We review the recently proposed reciprocal-space confinement theory, which predicts an exponential increase of resistivity with decreasing thickness at the nanoscale, and discuss how it can be combined with classical surface-scattering models to provide a unified description of ultra-thin metallic and semiconducting films. Finally, we summarize recent experimental evidence supporting this picture and discuss its implications for future nanoelectronic devices, nanoscale interconnects, and quantum transport under extreme spatial confinement.

AI.tldr: This review examines the transition from classical size effects (Fuchs-Sondheimer and Mayadas-Shatzkes models) to quantum confinement in ultra-thin films, introducing reciprocal-space confinement theory that predicts exponential resistivity increase at nanoscale, and proposes a unified framework combining quantum and classical scattering for future nanoelectronics.
AI.motivation: Classical models (Fuchs-Sondheimer and Mayadas-Shatzkes) fail to describe electrical resistivity in ultra-thin films under extreme confinement, as growing experimental evidence shows deviations from their predictions when film thickness is reduced to a few nanometers.
AI.method: The paper reviews the reciprocal-space confinement theory, which describes quantum-confinement effects that restructure electronic states available for transport, and discusses its integration with classical surface-scattering models (Fuchs-Sondheimer) to form a unified description.
AI.result: The reciprocal-space confinement theory predicts an exponential increase of resistivity with decreasing thickness at the nanoscale, going beyond the classical linear or power-law dependencies predicted by earlier models.
AI.conclusion: A unified framework combining quantum confinement with classical scattering can explain transport in ultra-thin metallic and semiconducting films, with significant implications for nanoelectronic devices, nanoscale interconnects, and quantum transport under extreme spatial confinement.

title: Benchmarking SOPPA-based methods for the calculation of static and dynamic polarizabilities
summary: Static and frequency-dependent polarizabilities were computed for 41 molecules using RPA, RPA(D), HRPA, HRPA(D), SOPPA, SOPPA(CC2), and SOPPA(CCSD) with the aug-cc-pVTZ basis set and benchmarked against CCSD reference values and available experimental data. The analysis reveals a pronounced distinction between the performance of these methods for aromatic versus non-aromatic molecules. Across all frequencies, HRPA consistently yields substantially larger deviations from CCSD than the other approaches, whereas HRPA(D) and SOPPA(CCSD) provide the most accurate results overall.
