For static polarizabilities, HRPA(D) performs best for non-aromatic systems, followed by SOPPA(CCSD) and RPA(D), while SOPPA(CCSD) is most accurate for aromatic molecules. In the frequency-dependent regime, HRPA(D) remains the most accurate method for non-aromatic molecules, although RPA(D) shows greater consistency. For aromatic molecules, SOPPA(CCSD) performs best at low frequencies, with RPA offering intermediate accuracy but higher consistency than most other methods; at higher frequencies, RPA becomes the most accurate approach, followed by RPA(D), while SOPPA(CCSD) deteriorates. These trends highlight the importance of doubles corrections in RPA(D) and HRPA(D), which achieve accuracy comparable to or better than SOPPA(CCSD) at lower computational cost. The strong performance of RPA for aromatic molecules is attributed to its characteristic overestimation of the lowest electronic excitation energy. Comparison with experimental data confirms SOPPA(CCSD) as the most reliable method for static polarizabilities, while RPA and HRPA(D) provide the best agreement for frequency-dependent polarizabilities of aromatic systems.

AI.tldr: This study benchmarks polarizabilities for 41 molecules using various ab initio methods against CCSD and experimental data, finding that HRPA(D) and SOPPA(CCSD) are most accurate overall, with clear performance differences between aromatic and non-aromatic molecules, and RPA performing well for aromatic systems due to its overestimation of excitation energies.
AI.motivation: To evaluate and compare the accuracy of several computationally efficient methods (RPA, RPA(D), HRPA, HRPA(D), SOPPA, SOPPA(CC2), SOPPA(CCSD)) for computing static and frequency-dependent polarizabilities, benchmarked against high-level CCSD and experimental data, especially to understand performance differences between aromatic and non-aromatic molecules.
AI.method: Static and frequency-dependent polarizabilities were computed for 41 molecules using RPA, RPA(D), HRPA, HRPA(D), SOPPA, SOPPA(CC2), and SOPPA(CCSD) with the aug-cc-pVTZ basis set, benchmarked against CCSD reference values and experimental data.
AI.result: HRPA(D) and SOPPA(CCSD) provide the most accurate results overall. For static polarizabilities, HRPA(D) is best for non-aromatic systems, SOPPA(CCSD) for aromatic molecules. For frequency-dependent polarizabilities, HRPA(D) is most accurate for non-aromatic molecules; for aromatics, SOPPA(CCSD) is best at low frequencies while RPA is most accurate at high frequencies. RPA(D) and HRPA(D) achieve accuracy comparable to or better than SOPPA(CCSD) at lower computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Doubles corrections in RPA(D) and HRPA(D) yield accuracy competitive with SOPPA(CCSD) at lower cost. SOPPA(CCSD) is most reliable for static polarizabilities, while RPA and HRPA(D) provide the best agreement with frequency-dependent experimental data for aromatic systems. Method choice should consider molecular aromaticity and frequency regime.

title: Exact amplitude relations for diffusion-limited aggregation
summary: It has been known for several decades that the third moment of the multifractal spectrum of the harmonic measure for diffusion-limited aggregates is linked to the underlying fractal dimension of the cluster. We demonstrate, using an argument based on the Hastings-Levitov formulation of diffusion-limited aggregation (DLA) in two dimensions, an even stronger link, connecting the universal amplitude of the third moment to the cluster fractal dimension. This argument can be used for both the standard circular DLA as well as DLA in a cylinder (i.e., with periodic boundary conditions).

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates a universal link between the third moment of the multifractal spectrum of harmonic measure and the fractal dimension of DLA clusters, using the Hastings-Levitov formulation in two dimensions, applicable to both circular and cylindrical geometries.
AI.motivation: To establish a stronger, universal connection between the amplitude of the third multifractal moment and the fractal dimension of DLA clusters, going beyond previously known relationships.
AI.method: The authors use an argument based on the Hastings-Levitov formulation of diffusion-limited aggregation (DLA) in two dimensions, analyzing both standard circular DLA and DLA in a cylinder (periodic boundary conditions).
AI.result: A universal link connecting the amplitude of the third moment of the multifractal spectrum of harmonic measure to the cluster fractal dimension is demonstrated.
AI.conclusion: The third moment's universal amplitude is strongly linked to the fractal dimension of DLA clusters, valid for both circular and cylindrical geometries.

title: Efficient Large-Scale STEM-EELS Simulations With Torched-TACAW
summary: The time auto-correlation of auxiliary wave functions (TACAW) method enables efficient simulations of ultra-low-loss electron energy loss spectra (EELS) arising from vibrational and magnon excitations. In practical applications to realistic materials systems, however, TACAW calculations become challenging due to the large system sizes required for models containing defects, interfaces, impurities, or grain boundaries, as well as the substantial computational cost and data throughput associated with molecular dynamics and multislice calculations. Here we discuss a practical methodology for large-scale TACAW simulations and present torched-TACAW, a freely available implementation of the TACAW part of the described workflow for efficient STEM-EELS simulations. The overall approach combines molecular dynamics based on foundational machine-learned interatomic potentials, partitioning of elongated supercells, and on-the-fly processing of multislice outputs in order to enable near ab initio quality simulations with tractable memory use and data flow. Using rutile TiO2 as a model system, we analyze important numerical aspects of the method, including windowing and supercell partitioning, and demonstrate atomic-resolution STEM-EELS simulations for thick samples.

AI.tldr: The paper presents torched-TACAW, an efficient implementation of the TACAW method for large-scale STEM-EELS simulations combining machine-learned interatomic potentials, supercell partitioning, and on-the-fly multislice processing to enable near ab initio quality ultra-low-loss EELS simulations with tractable memory use.
AI.motivation: TACAW calculations for ultra-low-loss EELS become challenging for realistic material systems with defects, interfaces, impurities, or grain boundaries due to large system sizes and high computational/data throughput costs associated with molecular dynamics and multislice calculations.
AI.method: The methodology combines (1) molecular dynamics using foundational machine-learned interatomic potentials, (2) partitioning of elongated supercells, and (3) on-the-fly processing of multislice outputs, implemented in the open-source torched-TACAW code.
AI.result: Using rutile TiO2 as a model system, the authors analyze numerical aspects such as windowing and supercell partitioning, and demonstrate atomic-resolution STEM-EELS simulations for thick samples with near ab initio quality.
AI.conclusion: The torched-TACAW implementation enables practical large-scale TACAW simulations with tractable memory use and data flow, making ultra-low-loss EELS simulations feasible for complex realistic material systems.

title: Ultrasonic Observation of Slowing Down of Multipole Fluctuations in Sr$_2$RuO$_4$
summary: We performed ultrasonic measurements on the unconventional superconductor Sr$_2$RuO$_4$ to investigate the dynamical properties of the electronic states near its superconducting transition temperature, $T_\mathrm{c} = 1.4$ K. We observed an increase in the in-plane transverse ultrasonic attenuation coefficient as the temperature approached $T_\mathrm{c}$. The ultrasonic attenuation exhibited a Landau-Khalatnikov-type ultrasonic frequency dependence with a typical relaxation time of approximately $10^{-10}$ s. Under an applied magnetic field of 10 T, the superconducting transition was suppressed. However, the ultrasonic attenuation coefficient exhibited an increase down to low temperatures, indicating the slowing down of fluctuations associated with multipole degrees of freedom. Based on group-theoretical considerations, we propose that the electric hexadecapole plays a crucial role in the slowing down. Furthermore, we discuss the relationship between multi-component superconducting order parameters and multipole degrees of freedom.

AI.tldr: Ultrasonic measurements on Sr₂RuO₄ reveal critical slowing down of hexadecapole fluctuations near Tc (~1.4 K), with Landau-Khalatnikov-type relaxation (~10⁻¹⁰ s), suggesting coupling between multipole degrees of freedom and multi-component superconducting order parameters.
AI.motivation: To investigate the dynamical properties of electronic states near Tc in the unconventional superconductor Sr₂RuO₄, particularly focusing on fluctuation phenomena associated with multipole degrees of freedom.
AI.method: In-plane transverse ultrasonic attenuation measurements on Sr₂RuO₄ single crystals across Tc (1.4 K), with frequency-dependent analysis and magnetic field (10 T) suppression of superconductivity, combined with group-theoretical analysis.
AI.result: Observed increased ultrasonic attenuation near Tc exhibiting Landau-Khalatnikov-type frequency dependence with relaxation time ~10⁻¹⁰ s; under 10 T field, attenuation continued to increase at low temperatures, indicating slowing down of multipole fluctuations; identified electric hexadecapole as the relevant degree of freedom.
AI.conclusion: Electric hexadecapole fluctuations play a crucial role in the observed critical slowing down; there is a meaningful relationship between multi-component superconducting order parameters and multipole degrees of freedom in Sr₂RuO₄.

title: An efficient formalism for inertial spin waves: Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya antiferromagnets as case studies
summary: Magnetic inertia, emerging in the ultrafast regime, supports inertial spin waves (SWs) as novel magnetic excitations. Despite considerable efforts devoted to inertial SWs, a systematic formalism for fully characterizing their intrinsic properties, especially chirality and polarization, is still lacking, and inertial SWs in spatially nonuniform magnetic configurations remain poorly explored. Here, we develop a framework for calculating inertial SWs and establish a general definition of their chirality and polarization via the ellipticity angle, a unified parameter encoding frequency sign, phase difference, and elliptical axis ratio. Using this method, we systematically investigate precessional and nutational SWs in uniaxial antiferromagnets with staggered and homogeneous Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions (DMIs), covering uniform collinear, canted, and spiral magnetic configurations. The results reveal that small staggered DMI preserves spin-wave degeneracy, whereas small homogeneous DMI lifts it. Further space-time inversion symmetry breaking in canted and spiral structures fully removes spin-wave degeneracy across the entire Brillouin zone. Long-wavelength nutational SWs behave as backward waves, and flat bands emerge in canted and spiral configurations near a critical inertial relaxation time. In canted and spiral configurations, nutational modes are always lefthanded whereas precessional modes are always righthanded; additionally, the dispersion spectra of the canted configuration can be derived from those of the spiral configuration via band folding. Polarization is wavenumber insensitive for uniform configurations but becomes strongly dispersive for nonuniform ones. This work advances the fundamental understanding of magnetic inertial dynamics and provides theoretical insights for the development of ultrafast magnonic devices.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a theoretical framework for characterizing inertial spin waves in antiferromagnets, introducing a general definition of chirality and polarization via ellipticity angle, and reveals how Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions and magnetic configurations affect spin-wave degeneracy, handedness, and dispersion.
AI.motivation: A systematic formalism for fully characterizing intrinsic properties of inertial spin waves (especially chirality and polarization) was lacking, and inertial SWs in spatially nonuniform magnetic configurations remained poorly explored.
AI.method: The authors develop a framework for calculating inertial spin waves and define chirality and polarization via the ellipticity angle—a unified parameter encoding frequency sign, phase difference, and elliptical axis ratio. They investigate precessional and nutational SWs in uniaxial antiferromagnets with staggered and homogeneous DMIs across uniform collinear, canted, and spiral magnetic configurations.
AI.result: Small staggered DMI preserves spin-wave degeneracy; small homogeneous DMI lifts it. Space-time inversion symmetry breaking in canted/spiral structures fully removes degeneracy across the Brillouin zone. Long-wavelength nutational SWs behave as backward waves. Flat bands emerge near critical inertial relaxation time in canted/spiral configurations. Nutational modes are always left-handed; precessional modes always right-handed in canted/spiral configurations. Polarization is wavenumber insensitive for uniform configurations but strongly dispersive for nonuniform ones.
AI.conclusion: This work advances fundamental understanding of magnetic inertial dynamics and provides theoretical insights for developing ultrafast magnonic devices.

title: Nonperturbative Nonlinear Hall Effect in Nonequilibrium Steady States
summary: The nonlinear Hall effect in quantum materials has attracted broad interest, yet most existing studies focus on the weak-field, perturbative regime. Here we develop a nonperturbative approach based on nonequilibrium steady-state Green's functions for dc-field-driven lattice systems, with dissipation and interactions incorporated through self-energies beyond the constant relaxation-time approximation and interband transitions treated alongside their intraband counterparts. Applied to a two-band semimetal model, our approach provides direct access to the strong-field Hall response beyond the nonperturbative crossover where the edge of the nonequilibrium distribution reaches Berry-curvature hot spots, a regime in which constant relaxation-time estimates and Berry curvature dipole calculations become unreliable. We further demonstrate that interaction and electron-phonon self-energies within dynamical mean-field theory can substantially change the Hall signal. Our framework enables quantitative simulations of nonequilibrium nonlinear Hall phenomena and provides guidance for strong-field transport experiments.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a nonperturbative approach using nonequilibrium steady-state Green's functions to study the nonlinear Hall effect in strong dc fields, going beyond weak-field perturbative methods. Applied to a two-band semimetal, it reveals regimes where constant relaxation-time and Berry curvature dipole approximations fail, and shows that interaction/electron-phonon self-energies significantly affect the Hall signal.
AI.motivation: Existing studies of the nonlinear Hall effect focus on the weak-field perturbative regime, leaving the strong-field nonperturbative regime largely unexplored due to the lack of suitable theoretical frameworks.
AI.method: The authors develop a nonperturbative approach based on nonequilibrium steady-state Green's functions for dc-field-driven lattice systems, incorporating dissipation and interactions via self-energies that go beyond the constant relaxation-time approximation, and treating both interband and intraband transitions.
AI.result: Applied to a two-band semimetal, the approach captures the strong-field Hall response beyond the nonperturbative crossover where the nonequilibrium distribution reaches Berry-curvature hot spots. It shows that constant relaxation-time estimates and Berry curvature dipole calculations become unreliable in this regime, and that interaction and electron-phonon self-energies within dynamical mean-field theory substantially modify the Hall signal.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables quantitative simulations of nonequilibrium nonlinear Hall phenomena and provides guidance for strong-field transport experiments.

title: Phase-selective orbital-charge conversion in $\mathrm{MoTe_2}$
summary: Two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have emerged as promising materials for spin--orbitronics owing to their strong spin--orbit coupling and rich electronic phases. However, their orbital transport properties remain largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate that the orbitronic response of $\mathrm{MoTe_2}$ is governed by a thickness-driven structural phase transition. RF-sputtered $\mathrm{MoTe_2}$ thin films exhibit a crossover at a critical thickness of approximately $4.5\,\mathrm{nm}$, stabilizing in the metallic $1T^\prime$ phase below this threshold and in the semiconducting $2H$ phase above it. Raman spectroscopy and scanning tunneling spectroscopy (STS) confirm the structural and electronic transition, revealing gapless behavior in ultrathin films and a finite band gap in thicker samples. Spin-pumping measurements detect an additional transverse charge-conversion signal exclusively in metallic $1T^\prime$-$\mathrm{MoTe_2}$, in agreement with first-principles calculations that identify a dominant orbital Rashba--Edelstein response as the underlying conversion mechanism.

AI.tldr: MoTe₂ thin films exhibit a thickness-driven structural phase transition at ~4.5 nm, switching from metallic 1T′ (ultrathin) to semiconducting 2H (thicker) phases. The metallic 1T′ phase shows an additional transverse charge-conversion signal from spin pumping, attributed to an orbital Rashba–Edelstein mechanism, highlighting thickness-tunable orbitronic properties.
AI.motivation: Orbital transport properties in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) remain largely unexplored, despite their strong spin–orbit coupling and relevance to spin–orbitronics.
AI.method: RF-sputtered MoTe₂ thin films were studied across thicknesses; structural and electronic characterization via Raman spectroscopy and scanning tunneling spectroscopy (STS); spin-pumping measurements combined with first-principles calculations to identify the charge-conversion mechanism.
AI.result: A thickness-driven structural phase transition at ~4.5 nm: metallic 1T′ phase below, semiconducting 2H phase above. Only metallic 1T′‑MoTe₂ exhibits an additional transverse charge-conversion signal under spin pumping, consistent with a dominant orbital Rashba–Edelstein response.
AI.conclusion: Orbitronic response in MoTe₂ is governed by a structural phase transition tunable by film thickness, with the metallic 1T′ phase enabling a strong orbital Rashba–Edelstein conversion mechanism.

title: Differentiable inverse design of short-range order in high-entropy alloys: from target sro to target property
summary: Short-range order (SRO) governs the mechanical response of multi-principal-element alloys, but designing an alloy for a target property usually means solving two disconnected problems: building a structure matching a desired SRO pattern, then separately checking its property, with no shared optimization. This work replaces the standard random-swap search (reverse Monte Carlo) with a gradient-based approach: atom occupancy is treated as continuous rather than fixed, so the whole process can be tuned using gradient descent, the same method used to train neural networks. This builder matches random-swap accuracy on small systems, but is six times faster and eight times more accurate on large 4000-atom systems, and scales smoothly to alloys with many elements without extra bookkeeping. A physics-based correction term, adapted from prior two-element work and extended here to many elements, keeps designed structures thermodynamically realistic rather than just numerically matching the target SRO pattern. A small neural network then predicts mechanical properties directly from composition and SRO statistics, closing the loop from target property back to structure. Tested on nine face-centered-cubic and body-centered-cubic alloys, the pipeline captured SRO-driven stiffness changes from -20% to +57%, and cell-size checks showed at least 864 atoms are needed to get the direction and size of these changes right, since the commonly used 108-atom cells can mislead. Against real simulations for a cobalt-chromium-nickel alloy, the method matched three of four target stiffness values within 6%. The method is released as an open-source Python package, anisro, offering a practical route to gradient-based, property-driven alloy design.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a gradient-based approach to design multi-principal-element alloys with desired short-range order (SRO) and mechanical properties, replacing traditional random-swap methods. The method treats atom occupancy as continuous variables, uses gradient descent for faster and more accurate structure building, incorporates a physics-based correction term for thermodynamic realism, and employs a small neural network to predict stiffness from composition and SRO statistics. The open-source Python package, anisro, demonstrates up to 8× better accuracy on large systems and captures SRO-driven stiffness changes from -20% to +57% across nine alloys.
AI.motivation: Designing alloys for target properties requires solving two disconnected problems—building a structure matching a desired SRO pattern and separately checking its property—with no shared optimization. This disconnect motivates a unified, gradient-based framework that can close the loop from target property back to structure.
AI.method: The method replaces random-swap search (reverse Monte Carlo) with gradient-based optimization by treating atom occupancy as continuous variables, enabling gradient descent tuning. It includes a physics-based correction term (extended from two-element to many-element alloys) for thermodynamic realism, and a small neural network that predicts mechanical properties directly from composition and SRO statistics.
AI.result: On 4000-atom systems, the method is six times faster and eight times more accurate than random-swap search. Across nine FCC and BCC alloys, the pipeline captured SRO-driven stiffness changes from -20% to +57%. For a Co-Cr-Ni alloy, three of four target stiffness values were matched within 6%. Cell-size checks revealed at least 864 atoms are needed to correctly capture SRO effects.
AI.conclusion: The gradient-based approach offers a practical, scalable, and accurate route to property-driven alloy design, released as the open-source Python package anisro.

title: On the Symplectic Propagation of the Spin-MInt Algorithm for Non-Adiabatic Quantum Dynamics
comment: 45 pages, 2 figures, submitted to Journal of Mathematical Chemistry
summary: Mapping methods are often used for the numerical simulation of nonadiabatic systems by propagating classical mapping variable trajectories. A recently popularised mapping method is spin-mapping, whose mapping variables arise from quantum mechanical operators with symmetries described by a Lie-Poisson algebra. Simulating the classical-like dynamics of spin-mapping systems accurately is generally challenging, with many methods unable to preserve the underlying geometric structure of the symplectic form. The Spin-MInt algorithm is a recently proposed algorithm propagating spin-mapping variables, with a direct proof of symplecticity existing only for 2 electronic states. Here, we directly prove the symplecticity of the Spin-MInt algorithm for a general $K$ electronic states. A review of the symplectic nature of coadjoint orbits of the $\mathfrak{su}(K)$ Lie-Poisson algebra provides the framework needed to understand symplecticity of the Spin-MInt algorithm in this general case. The symplecticity of the method on the associated coadjoint orbit is then shown for what we believe to be the first time via an explicit verification of the symplecticity condition $\mathbf{MJ}\mathbf{M}^\textrm{T}=\mathbf{J}$ exploiting the Lie-Poisson structure of the system. To our knowledge, this is the first time the monodromy matrix for the Spin-MInt algorithm has been explicitly stated using canonical coordinates on the coherent state manifold for a general number of states. We hope that this will assist the development of classical-like spin-mapping methods which might utilise elements of the monodromy matrix, and inform future work on similar symplectic algorithms for coupled and uncoupled Lie-Poisson systems.

AI.tldr: This paper provides the first direct proof of symplecticity for the Spin-MInt algorithm with a general K electronic states, using the Lie-Poisson structure of su(K) coadjoint orbits and verifying the symplecticity condition M J M^T = J.
AI.motivation: Spin-mapping methods are used for nonadiabatic dynamics simulation, but existing symplecticity proofs for the Spin-MInt algorithm were limited to only 2 electronic states. A general proof for K states was needed to establish the geometric structure preservation of the method.
AI.method: The authors review the symplectic nature of coadjoint orbits of the su(K) Lie-Poisson algebra, then explicitly verify the symplecticity condition M J M^T = J using canonical coordinates on the coherent state manifold for a general number of states K.
AI.result: The symplecticity of the Spin-MInt algorithm is proven for a general K electronic states via the Lie-Poisson structure. The monodromy matrix for the algorithm is explicitly stated using canonical coordinates on the coherent state manifold for the first time.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes the geometric foundation for spin-mapping methods with arbitrary numbers of states, and may inform future development of symplectic algorithms for coupled and uncoupled Lie-Poisson systems.

title: Alternative routes to universal diversity scaling in component systems: from proteomes to large language models
summary: Remarkably common statistical laws characterize the diversity scaling and its fluctuations across a wide range of complex "component systems". These regularities are often interpreted as signatures of an underlying innovation mechanism driving the growth of component diversity, but the basic ingredients necessary for their emergence remain poorly understood. In particular, from language and technological artifacts to genomes and gene expression patterns, the number of distinct components grows sublinearly with system size, while its variance scales approximately as the square of its mean. This behavior is consistent across diverse systems, raising the question of whether general constraints or emergent principles underlying diversity and innovation define the architectures of realizations with different numbers of components. To address this question, we derive analytical conditions for the joint emergence of these two diversity laws within a broad class of growth models, showing that they require a specific asymptotic dependence of the innovation probability on diversity and system size. We then demonstrate that the same macroscopic laws arise in a different class of models with latent heterogeneity, where quadratic fluctuation scaling always emerges asymptotically as a consequence of general statistical principles, essentially the law of total variance, without explicitly assuming an innovation mechanism or any specific rule for system assembly. We compare these predictions with empirical data from language, genomes, LEGO constructions, and texts generated by large language models. Our results show that empirical diversity scaling laws strongly constrain generative models but do not uniquely identify the mechanisms generating diversity, revealing a close correspondence between innovation-driven growth models and latent-variable descriptions.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates universal statistical laws governing diversity scaling across complex systems (language, genomes, LEGO, etc.), deriving conditions for their emergence in growth models and showing that quadratic variance scaling can arise from latent heterogeneity without explicit innovation mechanisms. Empirical data constrains generative models but does not uniquely identify underlying mechanisms.
AI.motivation: To understand whether general constraints or emergent principles underlie the remarkably consistent diversity scaling laws observed across diverse component systems, and to determine what these laws reveal about the mechanisms generating diversity.
AI.method: The authors derive analytical conditions for the joint emergence of two diversity laws (sublinear growth of distinct components and quadratic variance scaling) within growth models. They also analyze latent-variable models showing that quadratic fluctuation scaling emerges asymptotically from the law of total variance. Predictions are compared with empirical data from language, genomes, LEGO constructions, and LLM-generated texts.
AI.result: The joint emergence of sublinear diversity growth and quadratic variance scaling requires specific asymptotic dependence of innovation probability on diversity and system size. In latent-variable models, quadratic fluctuation scaling emerges automatically without assuming an innovation mechanism. Empirical data constrains but does not uniquely identify generative mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: Diversity scaling laws strongly constrain generative models but are insufficient to uniquely identify the mechanisms generating diversity, as both innovation-driven growth and latent-variable descriptions can produce the same macroscopic patterns.

title: Anisotropic tunneling through magnetic barriers in 8-Pmmn borophene
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures. Version to appear in Phys. Lett. A 2026
summary: We present a theoretical study of electron tunneling through a magnetic barrier in 8-Pmmn borophene, created by depositing two ferromagnetic strips on the borophene sheet. Using a low-energy effective Hamiltonian that captures the anisotropic Dirac spectrum, we solve the Dirac equation in three regions and impose wave-function continuity at the interfaces. From the resulting spinor solutions, we compute current densities and determine transmission and reflection probabilities as functions of incident energy, angle, and barrier parameters. The transmission exhibits strong anisotropy due to the tilted Dirac cones, with pronounced suppression for specific incident directions, suggesting directional filtering of carriers. We further calculate the conductance using the Landauer-Büttiker formalism, revealing that both magnetic strength and barrier width can tune the charge transport properties. The results demonstrate that engineered magnetic barriers in 8-Pmmn borophene enable precise control over electron flow, offering a platform for anisotropic transport control and tunable quantum devices. The interplay between the intrinsic anisotropy of borophene and external magnetic barriers provides rich opportunities to manipulate Dirac fermions in two-dimensional systems.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically studies electron tunneling through magnetic barriers in 8-Pmmn borophene, showing that the anisotropic Dirac cones enable directional filtering and tunable charge transport via magnetic field strength and barrier width.
AI.motivation: To understand how magnetic barriers can control electron flow in 8-Pmmn borophene, leveraging its anisotropic Dirac spectrum for directional filtering and tunable quantum transport.
AI.method: The authors use a low-energy effective Hamiltonian for anisotropic Dirac cones, solve the Dirac equation in three regions (barrier and two leads) with wave-function continuity, compute current densities, transmission/reflection probabilities, and conductance via the Landauer-Büttiker formalism.
AI.result: Transmission is strongly anisotropic with pronounced suppression along specific incident directions (directional filtering). Both magnetic barrier strength and width effectively tune transport properties.
AI.conclusion: Engineered magnetic barriers in 8-Pmmn borophene enable precise control of electron flow, providing a platform for anisotropic transport control and tunable quantum devices.

title: Intrinsically low thermal conductivity of stoichiometric lithium niobate:Experimental measurement and microscopic origin
summary: With the rapid development of integrated electro-optic and nonlinear optical devices based on lithium niobate (LiNbO$_3$, LN), thermal management is becoming a critical area of focus. However, experimental measurement of thermal transport in stoichiometric LiNbO$_3$ (sLN) remains scarce, and the intrinsic microscopic mechanisms remain to be established. Here, we combine the laser pump-probe technique of frequency-domain thermoreflectance (FDTR) with state-of-the-art machine-learned atomistic simulations to comprehensively investigate thermal transport in sLN. The measured and simulated room-temperature thermal conductivity ($κ$) values of sLN agree well, which are orders-of-magnitude lower than that of many classic and emerging semiconductors such as silicon. Furthermore, the temperature-dependent $κ$ exhibits a $T^{-α}$ scaling with $α$ near unity, suggesting that thermal transport is dominated by intrinsic phonon-phonon scattering. By comparing sLN with cubic boron arsenide (cBAs) which serves as an ultrahigh-$κ$ benchmark, we reveal that harmonic properties are not responsible for the low $κ$ of sLN, which feature phonon heat capacity and group velocities that are either higher than or comparable to those in cBAs. Instead, the low $κ$ originates from substantially stronger anharmonicity and larger scattering phase space. These two factors collectively suppress phonon lifetimes by 1-2 orders of magnitude, leading to a maximum phonon mean free path of approximately 140 nm. As a result, notable size effects emerge in thin-film sLN below 1 $μ$m, with $κ$ dropping to half the bulk value at 10 nm. Altogether, our findings establish a fundamental understanding of thermal transport in sLN and provide atomistic insights for thermal management in advanced lithium niobate technologies.

AI.tldr: This paper combines FDTR experiments and machine-learned atomistic simulations to investigate thermal transport in stoichiometric LiNbO₃ (sLN), revealing that its ultralow thermal conductivity (~orders of magnitude lower than Si) stems from strong anharmonicity and large scattering phase space rather than harmonic properties, with notable size effects emerging below 1 μm thickness.
AI.motivation: With rapid development of integrated electro-optic and nonlinear optical devices based on lithium niobate, thermal management becomes critical, yet experimental thermal transport measurements in sLN are scarce and the intrinsic microscopic mechanisms remain unclear.
AI.method: Combined frequency-domain thermoreflectance (FDTR) experiments with state-of-the-art machine-learned atomistic simulations to measure and compute thermal conductivity across temperatures; compared with cubic boron arsenide (cBAs) as an ultrahigh-κ benchmark.
AI.result: Measured and simulated room-temperature κ agree well and are orders-of-magnitude lower than silicon; temperature-dependent κ follows T^{-α} scaling with α≈1 (intrinsic phonon-phonon scattering); harmonic properties (heat capacity, group velocities) are not responsible; low κ originates from substantially stronger anharmonicity and larger scattering phase space, suppressing phonon lifetimes by 1-2 orders of magnitude (max MFP ≈140 nm); size effects appear below 1 μm with κ dropping to half bulk value at 10 nm.
AI.conclusion: Established fundamental understanding of thermal transport in sLN and provided atomistic insights for thermal management in advanced lithium niobate technologies.

title: Molecular interpretability of the bulk electrochemical impedance of concentrated electrolytes
comment: 13 manuscript pages with 6 figures; 2 pages methods and 1 figure; 100 references+footnotes; 8 pages appendices including 5 figures and a table
summary: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) is a widely used technique to understand time-dependent response and relaxation under applied voltage. While these spectra contain a wealth of information, major gaps in our understanding can hinder our ability to interpret EIS spectra in terms of microscopic chemical mechanisms. We propose an alternative approach to common empirical fitting procedures for describing the contribution of the bulk electrolyte to the EIS spectrum. This new approach is rooted in determining the moments of the frequency-dependent conductivity, with molecular interpretability provided by a generalized Langevin equation description of an effective single particle dynamics; the `itinerant oscillator' (IO) model. In contrast to a Debye--Falkenhagen description, the IO model makes no assumptions regarding the concentration of the electrolyte, a fact we demonstrate by analysing molecular dynamics simulations of a room-temperature ionic liquid. By analysing the memory function from simulation within the framework provided by the IO model, we reveal the importance of capturing the separation of timescales within the memory function for describing the temperature dependent $β$-relaxation process. We go on to show how our impedance model directly reports on this distribution of timescales while retaining the simplicity of commonly employed workflows.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new approach to interpret electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) spectra by using the itinerant oscillator (IO) model and moments of frequency-dependent conductivity, moving beyond empirical fitting. It demonstrates the method's effectiveness on room-temperature ionic liquids, revealing the role of timescale separation in memory functions for β-relaxation processes.
AI.motivation: While EIS is widely used, major gaps exist in interpreting EIS spectra in terms of microscopic chemical mechanisms; common empirical fitting procedures are insufficient.
AI.method: The approach determines moments of frequency-dependent conductivity, with molecular interpretability provided by a generalized Langevin equation description of an effective single particle dynamics—the 'itinerant oscillator' (IO) model. Analysis of memory functions from molecular dynamics simulations is performed within the IO framework.
AI.result: Unlike Debye–Falkenhagen description, the IO model makes no assumptions about electrolyte concentration, demonstrated by analyzing MD simulations of room-temperature ionic liquids. Capturing timescale separation within the memory function is crucial for describing temperature-dependent β-relaxation.
AI.conclusion: The impedance model directly reports on the distribution of timescales while retaining the simplicity of commonly employed workflows, offering a physically grounded alternative to empirical fitting.

title: How wrong is too wrong: A numerical study on the relevance of positional memory in the generalized Langevin equation
summary: If a generalized Langevin equation contains a potential of mean force, it cannot at the same time contain a linear memory kernel and a fluctuating force that obeys a second fluctuation dissipation theorem in the sense of Kubo, and be exact. As modelers often prefer to use generalized Langevin equations that have the first three properties, one needs to ask how close the model dynamics is to the dynamics of the underlying microscopic system. To test this, we analyze a simple model system in which the potential of mean force can be well approximated by a polynomial of low order. The exact generalized Langevin equation of this model contains memory terms in addition to the linear one. We show that these additional terms, at least for the model system regarded in this article, are important for the dynamics and cannot be neglected if one intends to model core aspects of the underlying system correctly.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that generalized Langevin equations containing a potential of mean force, linear memory kernel, and Kubo-type fluctuation-dissipation theorem cannot be exact, and shows through a simple model that the additional nonlinear memory terms are crucial for accurate dynamics.
AI.motivation: Modelers often use generalized Langevin equations with three desirable properties (potential of mean force, linear memory kernel, Kubo's second fluctuation-dissipation theorem), but such equations cannot be exact. The authors aim to quantify how close these approximate model dynamics are to the true underlying microscopic dynamics.
AI.method: The authors analyze a simple model system where the potential of mean force is well approximated by a low-order polynomial. They derive the exact generalized Langevin equation for this model and compare it to the commonly used approximate form, examining the additional memory terms beyond the linear one.
AI.result: The exact generalized Langevin equation contains nonlinear memory terms in addition to the standard linear memory kernel. For the model system studied, these additional terms significantly impact the dynamics and cannot be neglected.
AI.conclusion: When using generalized Langevin equations with the three common properties, the additional nonlinear memory terms are important for correctly modeling core aspects of the underlying system and should not be ignored.

title: The Wigner function for Integer quantum Hall effect
summary: Wigner's quasi-probability distribution function in phase space is a specialized representation of the density matrix, possessing significant physical importance. In this article, we first review the wave function describing electronic motion in an electromagnetic field under the Landau gauge. Next, based on an introduction to the properties of the Wigner function, we calculate the Wigner function for the integer quantum Hall effect using the integral method.

AI.tldr: The paper reviews the wave function for electronic motion in an electromagnetic field under Landau gauge and calculates the Wigner function for the integer quantum Hall effect using the integral method.
AI.motivation: To provide a specialized representation of the density matrix via the Wigner quasi-probability distribution function and explore its physical significance in the context of the integer quantum Hall effect.
AI.method: Review of wave functions under Landau gauge, introduction to Wigner function properties, and calculation of the Wigner function for the integer quantum Hall effect using the integral method.
AI.result: The calculated Wigner function for the integer quantum Hall effect using the integral method.
AI.conclusion: The Wigner function provides a valuable phase-space representation for understanding the integer quantum Hall effect.

title: Evidence for Deconfined Magnetic Order in the Kitaev-$J_3$ Model
summary: We investigate the Kitaev-$J_3$ honeycomb model using variational Monte Carlo calculations combined with a vison-quasiparticle analysis of the parent Kitaev spin liquid (KSL). We provide evidence for deconfined magnetic phases in which zigzag or antiferromagnetic order coexists with remnant $\mathbb{Z}_2$ topological structure inherited from the KSL. The optimized variational wave functions retain multiple linearly independent topological sectors on a torus, whereas those of conventional ordered phases collapse to a single sector. The vison-quasiparticle analysis shows that magnetic order naturally arises from vison-pair condensation while single visons remain gapped, yielding a microscopic mechanism for magnetic ordering without immediate confinement. The resulting phases further host gapless spinons with multiple Majorana cones, offering a possible microscopic scenario for the anomalous low-temperature longitudinal thermal transport reported in magnetically ordered Kitaev materials such as Na$_2$Co$_2$TeO$_6$. Our results reveal a microscopic route to fractionalized magnetism beyond the conventional dichotomy between magnetic order and spin-liquid behavior.

Magnetic order arises from vison-pair condensation while single visons remain gapped, producing gapless spinons with multiple Majorana cones that may explain anomalous thermal transport in Kitaev materials like Na$_2$Co$_2$TeO$_6$.
AI.motivation: To understand how magnetic order can emerge from a Kitaev spin liquid without immediate confinement, and to explain anomalous low-temperature longitudinal thermal transport observed in magnetically ordered Kitaev materials such as Na$_2$Co$_2$TeO$_6$.
AI.method: Variational Monte Carlo calculations combined with a vison-quasiparticle analysis of the parent Kitaev spin liquid.
AI.result: Deconfined magnetic phases exist where zigzag or antiferromagnetic order coexists with remnant $\mathbb{Z}_2$ topological structure. The optimized variational wave functions retain multiple linearly independent topological sectors on a torus, while conventional ordered phases collapse to a single sector. Magnetic order arises from vison-pair condensation with gapped single visons, and the phases host gapless spinons with multiple Majorana cones.
