title: Many-body benchmarking of DFT local-registry energetics in bilayer InSe
summary: Density functional theory (DFT) is widely used to model twisted bilayers, but the accuracy of the local stacking energetics underlying such models remains uncertain. Here, we benchmark the local-registry landscape of bilayer InSe using diffusion quantum Monte Carlo (DMC). DFT predicts that AB, AAr, and ABr stackings, which share the same interfacial Se registry, are nearly degenerate within 1.5 meV/f.u. and exhibit nearly indistinguishable DFT charge-density responses. DMC instead separates these stackings by 8(5) and 41(4) meV/f.u., while the energy difference between the most stable and least stable registries reaches 60(7) meV/f.u.. These large energy separations show that the stacking energetics are not determined by the interfacial atomic motif alone but depend on the full registry and its associated many-body electronic response. More broadly, these results show that DFT-based moiré models can substantially underestimate local stacking-energy corrugation, with direct consequences for predicted structural relaxation, domain formation, and electronic reconstruction in twisted layered materials.

AI.tldr: DFT underestimates local stacking-energy corrugation in twisted bilayer InSe compared to DMC benchmarks, showing that stacking energetics depend on full registry and many-body electronic response, not just interfacial atomic motifs.
AI.motivation: To benchmark the accuracy of DFT for modeling local stacking energetics in twisted bilayers, specifically bilayer InSe, as this directly affects moiré model predictions for structural relaxation, domain formation, and electronic reconstruction.
AI.method: The authors benchmark the local-registry landscape of bilayer InSe using diffusion quantum Monte Carlo (DMC) and compare with DFT predictions, analyzing stacking energies and charge-density responses for different stacking configurations (AB, AAr, ABr).
AI.result: DFT predicts near degeneracy (~1.5 meV/f.u.) for AB, AAr, and ABr stackings with similar charge-density responses, while DMC separates them by 8(5) and 41(4) meV/f.u., with total stacking energy corrugation reaching 60(7) meV/f.u..
AI.conclusion: Stacking energetics depend on full registry and many-body electronic response, not just interfacial atomic motifs. DFT-based moiré models can substantially underestimate local stacking-energy corrugation, affecting predictions of structural relaxation, domain formation, and electronic reconstruction in twisted layered materials.

title: On the emergence of quantum many-body chaos for tunably-broken integrability
summary: We develop a quantitative theory for the emergence of quantum many-body chaos as integrability is broken via a tunable parameter. In a circuit model of free fermions, 'doped' with a tunable density of integrability-breaking gates, we uncover the microscopic mechanisms underpinning the crossover from early-time integrable behaviour to late-time chaos through the lens of the out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs). The integrability-breaking gates act as local, in spacetime, hotspots which locally amplify the OTOCs such that an accumulation of them eventually leads to fully-developed chaos. We identify the explicit characteristic time and length scales governing this crossover, as well as the dependence of the chaotic OTOC characteristics -- such as the butterfly velocity and front broadening -- on the integrability-breaking parameter.

AI.tldr: A quantitative theory of how quantum many-body chaos emerges when integrability is broken in a tunable circuit model of free fermions, revealing microscopic mechanisms behind the crossover from integrable to chaotic behavior via OTOC analysis.
AI.motivation: To understand the microscopic mechanisms by which quantum many-body chaos emerges as integrability is broken, and to quantify the characteristic scales governing the crossover from integrable to chaotic dynamics.
AI.method: A circuit model of free fermions doped with tunable density of integrability-breaking gates, analyzed through the lens of out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs).
AI.result: Identified explicit characteristic time and length scales governing the crossover, as well as the dependence of chaotic OTOC characteristics (butterfly velocity, front broadening) on the integrability-breaking parameter. Integrability-breaking gates act as local spacetime hotspots that amplify OTOCs, leading to fully-developed chaos.
AI.conclusion: The accumulation of local integrability-breaking hotspots drives the crossover from early-time integrable behavior to late-time chaos, with quantitatively characterized scales and parameter dependence.

title: Velocity and force autocorrelations in Brownian dynamics with a Lorentz force
summary:
We derive a general relation between the velocity and force autocorrelation tensors (VACT and FACT) for a Brownian particle subject to an external magnetic field. Using time-symmetry arguments, we show that, for the full Langevin dynamics, the VACT depends only on the FACT, independently of the details of the interaction potential. Under the hypothesis of timescale separation between thermalization and interaction-driven motion, this relation simplifies considerably in the overdamped (Brownian) limit. A central feature of the overdamped result is that, unlike in the field-free case, the part of the VACT that controls the self-diffusion of the particle couples to the antisymmetric part of the FACT, with a coupling strength set by the ratio of the cyclotron frequency to the thermalization rate. We validate and illustrate the formalism on an exactly solvable model: a dimer of charged particles bound by a harmonic potential. Depending on the relative sign of the particle charges, the magnetic field is found to produce either a transient suppression of mobility and diffusion that is fully recovered at long times, or a persistent oscillatory force autocorrelation, regions of negative mobility, and a
  long-time suppression of self-diffusion.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a general relationship between velocity and force autocorrelation tensors for Brownian particles in a magnetic field, showing that the overdamped limit couples self-diffusion to the antisymmetric part of the force autocorrelation tensor, with applications to a dimer model revealing either transient or persistent magnetic effects on diffusion.
AI.motivation: To understand how an external magnetic field modifies the diffusion and mobility of Brownian particles, specifically deriving general relations between velocity and force autocorrelation tensors that go beyond the field-free case.
AI.method: Using time-symmetry arguments for full Langevin dynamics, deriving a general VACT-FACT relation independent of interaction details, then simplifying under overdamped limit via timescale separation. Validated on an exactly solvable harmonic dimer model.
AI.result: In the overdamped limit, the VACT controlling self-diffusion couples to the antisymmetric part of the FACT with coupling strength proportional to the cyclotron frequency-to-thermalization rate ratio. The dimer model shows two regimes: transient suppression of mobility fully recovered at long times, or persistent oscillatory FACT, negative mobility regions, and long-time diffusion suppression.
AI.conclusion: The magnetic field introduces fundamental changes to Brownian motion statistics via coupling to antisymmetric force correlations, with observable consequences for self-diffusion that depend on charge sign combinations.

title: Quantum-geometric shift of quasiequilibrium: Origin of nonreciprocal current driven by quantum-metric dipole
summary: We study nonlinear DC electric transport of quantum-metric origin by combining adiabatic perturbation theory with the nonequilibrium Green function approach. The adiabatic ansatz provides a basis for directly treating a DC electric field in the velocity gauge, rather than introducing it as the zero-frequency limit of an AC field. The resulting adiabatic-basis Hamiltonian takes the same form as in the length gauge, enabling a systematic comparison across different formulations. Applying this fully quantum formulation, we find a longitudinal nonreciprocal current governed by the quantum-metric dipole. The essential ingredient is a quantum correction to the distribution function that is absent in semiclassical treatments. We trace this correction to the finite spread of an electron wave packet during relaxation under a bias field, thereby identifying shifted quasiequilibrium as the physical origin of quantum-metric nonreciprocal transport.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a fully quantum formulation of nonlinear DC transport originating from quantum geometry, showing that longitudinal nonreciprocal current is governed by the quantum-metric dipole, with the key ingredient being a quantum correction to the distribution function linked to wave-packet spread during relaxation under bias—identified as shifted quasiequilibrium.
AI.motivation: To understand nonlinear DC electric transport of quantum-metric origin using a fully quantum approach that avoids the zero-frequency limit of AC fields, and to resolve the physical origin of such transport.
AI.method: Combines adiabatic perturbation theory with the nonequilibrium Green function approach; treats DC electric field directly in the velocity gauge via adiabatic ansatz; derives adiabatic-basis Hamiltonian that matches the length-gauge form.
AI.result: Finds a longitudinal nonreciprocal current governed by the quantum-metric dipole; identifies a quantum correction to the distribution function absent in semiclassical treatments as the essential ingredient.
AI.conclusion: The quantum correction arises from finite wave-packet spread during relaxation under bias, identifying shifted quasiequilibrium as the physical origin of quantum-metric nonreciprocal transport.

title: Plaid-Like Spin Splitting and Chirality of Magnon Bands in Antiferromagnetic MnTe$_2$
summary: Altermagnets constitute an emerging class of magnetic materials that combine compensated antiferromagnetic order with spin-split excitations arising from crystalline symmetries. Despite strong theoretical interest, their experimental identification remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate that helicity- and angle-resolved Raman scattering measurements reveal reduced rotational symmetries of magnons and a pronounced imbalance between left- and right-circular polarization channels, indicating momentum-dependent magnon handedness. First-principles DFT+$U$ calculations combined with linear spin-wave theory uncover a characteristic plaid-like spin-splitting structure in momentum space. The resulting magnon spin textures are dictated by the unconventional sublattice symmetries of MnTe$_2$ and closely emulate those of altermagnetic electronic bands. Our work provides evidence of chiral spin-wave excitations unique to this non-coplanar antiferromagnet.

AI.tldr: Helicity- and angle-resolved Raman scattering in MnTe₂ reveals chiral magnons with reduced rotational symmetry and plaid-like spin-splitting, confirming altermagnetic behavior via first-principles calculations.
AI.motivation: Altermagnets are theoretically predicted but experimentally challenging to identify; this work aims to provide a clear experimental signature for altermagnetic magnon excitations.
AI.method: Helicity- and angle-resolved Raman scattering experiments combined with DFT+U calculations and linear spin-wave theory to probe magnon symmetries and spin textures in MnTe₂.
AI.result: Observation of reduced rotational symmetries of magnons and a strong circular dichroism imbalance; discovery of a plaid-like spin-splitting structure in momentum space with magnon handedness.
AI.conclusion: The work provides evidence of chiral spin-wave excitations unique to non-coplanar altermagnets, confirming that MnTe₂ hosts altermagnetic magnon bands analogous to electronic bands.

title: Contrarian Majority Dynamics: Violation of Detailed Balance and Nonequilibrium Steady States
summary: I revisit the Galam Majority Model (GMM) with contrarian agents from a statistical-mechanics perspective, revealing three fundamental features. First, in addition to the GMM simultaneous-update of small discussion groups, I construct a related single-agent stochastic dynamics, providing a Markovian microscopic representation, which is found to yield the same evolution equation. Second, I show that, contrary to what is often stated in the literature, the GMM closed evolution equation for the opinion density is not the result of a mean-field approximation. Indeed, I derive the conventional mean-field dynamics associated with majority-rule interactions and show that it yields a distinct, probabilistic evolution equation contrary the deterministic GMM equation. I therefore identify the GMM as an iterated mean-field dynamics. Third, I investigate the thermodynamic nature of the dynamics obtained from both single-agent and simultaneous updates. Both are shown to violate detailed balance. However, while Kolmogorov's cycle condition is satisfied for single-agent updates, it is violated for simultaneous updates, making the departure from equilibrium stronger in the latter case. I then compute the probability flux in the stationary state and show that it is non-vanishing, confirming the absence of an effective Hamiltonian and establishing that the stationary state is a genuine nonequilibrium steady state.These results clarify the statistical-mechanical foundations of the GMM and establish contrarian majority dynamics as an intrinsically non-equilibrium process with distinct regimes of irreversibility. Contrarians are not thermal noise.

AI.tldr: This paper revisits the Galam Majority Model (GMM) with contrarian agents, establishing its statistical-mechanical foundations. It shows the GMM is not a mean-field approximation but an iterated mean-field dynamics, and demonstrates that its dynamics violate detailed balance, making it a genuine nonequilibrium steady state with distinct irreversibility regimes.
AI.motivation: To clarify the statistical-mechanical foundations of the Galam Majority Model with contrarian agents, which have been misunderstood in the literature, particularly regarding its mean-field nature and thermodynamic properties.
AI.method: The author constructs a single-agent stochastic (Markovian) dynamics that yields the same evolution equation as the simultaneous-update GMM. Mean-field dynamics for majority-rule interactions are derived and compared. Detailed balance and Kolmogorov's cycle condition are analyzed for both update schemes. Probability flux in the stationary state is computed.
AI.result: (1) The single-agent Markovian dynamics reproduces the GMM evolution equation. (2) The conventional mean-field dynamics yields a probabilistic evolution equation distinct from the deterministic GMM equation, identifying GMM as an iterated mean-field dynamics rather than a standard mean-field approximation. (3) Both update schemes violate detailed balance; simultaneous updates also violate Kolmogorov's cycle condition (stronger nonequilibrium), while single-agent updates satisfy it. Non-vanishing probability flux confirms the absence of an effective Hamiltonian and establishes a genuine nonequilibrium steady state.
AI.conclusion: Contrarian majority dynamics is an intrinsically non-equilibrium process with distinct regimes of irreversibility. Contrarians are not equivalent to thermal noise.

title: Unconventional Mixed-Parity Magnetism in Rare-Earth Tetraborides
comment: Main manuscript: 10 pages, 4 figures, Supplementary Material: 12 pages, 11 figures, 1 table
summary: Altermagnetism has advanced the study of compensated magnets by revealing non-relativistic spin splitting, traditionally classified into strictly even- or odd-parity spin textures. Here, we unveil a fundamentally different regime: component-resolved mixed-parity spin splitting in a fully three-dimensional compensated magnet. Using first-principles calculations, tight-binding and $\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{p}$ models, along with spin-group symmetry analysis, we demonstrate that the non-coplanar ground state of $\mathrm{TbB}_4$ enforces a unique momentum-space spin texture. The in-plane spin components exhibit odd-parity $p$- and $f$-wave-like textures, whereas the out-of-plane component retains an even-parity $d$-wave altermagnetic character. Crucially, the coexistence of the in-plane odd-parity textures is driven not by relativistic spin-orbit coupling, but by a staggered Berry phase arising from the inherent scalar spin chirality. This mixed-parity structure dictates distinct transport fingerprints, including bulk non-relativistic Edelstein and spin Hall responses, as well as a symmetry-allowed Berry curvature dipole. These results establish the rare-earth tetraborides as a robust platform for engineering complex spin-charge conversion phenomena.

AI.tldr: This paper discovers component-resolved mixed-parity spin splitting in the three-dimensional compensated magnet TbB₄, where in-plane spins exhibit odd-parity textures while out-of-plane spins retain even-parity altermagnetic character, driven by scalar spin chirality rather than spin-orbit coupling, leading to distinct transport phenomena.
AI.motivation: To go beyond traditional even- or odd-parity spin textures in compensated magnets and explore a new regime of mixed-parity spin splitting in fully three-dimensional systems.
AI.method: First-principles calculations, tight-binding and k·p models, and spin-group symmetry analysis.
AI.result: Non-coplanar ground state of TbB₄ yields in-plane odd-parity p- and f-wave spin textures and out-of-plane even-parity d-wave altermagnetic texture; odd-parity textures arise from staggered Berry phase (scalar spin chirality), not spin-orbit coupling.
AI.conclusion: Rare-earth tetraborides serve as a robust platform for engineering complex spin-charge conversion, exhibiting bulk non-relativistic Edelstein and spin Hall effects and a symmetry-allowed Berry curvature dipole.

title: Density functional study of native point defects in CaO
summary: We investigate the structural, electronic, and optical properties of native point defects in CaO using first-principles density-functional calculations. Oxygen vacancies are favored under O-poor conditions, whereas calcium vacancies dominate under O-rich conditions. Calculated migration barriers and binding energies indicate that vacancy complexes are thermodynamically stable and can survive high-temperature annealing. Optical transition energies, evaluated using the Franck-Condon framework, suggest that several experimentally observed absorption and emission peaks can be attributed to negatively charged vacancy complexes as well as isolated oxygen vacancies.

AI.tldr: First-principles DFT study of native point defects in CaO shows oxygen vacancies are favored under O-poor conditions, calcium vacancies under O-rich; vacancy complexes are thermally stable; optical transitions from negatively charged complexes and isolated oxygen vacancies explain experimental peaks.
AI.motivation: To understand the structural, electronic, and optical properties of native point defects in CaO, which are critical for its performance as a wide-bandgap oxide in applications such as electronics and optics.
AI.method: First-principles density-functional theory (DFT) calculations, including migration barrier and binding energy analysis, and Franck-Condon framework for optical transition energies.
AI.result: Oxygen vacancies dominate under O-poor conditions; calcium vacancies under O-rich conditions. Vacancy complexes are thermodynamically stable and survive high-temperature annealing. Optical transitions from negatively charged vacancy complexes and isolated oxygen vacancies match experimental absorption and emission peaks.
AI.conclusion: The identified defect configurations and their optical signatures provide a consistent explanation for experimentally observed optical features in CaO, aiding in defect engineering for this material.

title: Correlation and entanglement dynamics of free fermions in disguise
summary: We study the nonequilibrium dynamics following a quantum quench in spin chains that can be solved via a mapping to free fermions in disguise. These models feature an exponential degeneracy of all energy eigenvalues, raising the question of the validity of the established framework describing the properties of integrable systems out of equilibrium. We present two main results. First, we develop an analytic method to compute the quasi-momentum distribution function characterizing the generalized Gibbs ensemble, and derive an analytic formula to compute the corresponding expectation values for special observables. Second, we conjecture a modification of the standard formula for the entanglement growth based on the quasi-particle picture, taking into account that each fermion in disguise carries an additional amount of entropy due to the exponential degeneracy of the energy eigenvalues. We test our theoretical predictions against numerical tensor-network computations for different initial states and Hamiltonian parameters. For the local observables, we find excellent agreement. For the entanglement dynamics, we find small deviations suggesting that our conjecture is only approximately correct. Our results represent a first step towards the extension of the established framework of integrable systems out of equilibrium to models hosting free fermions in disguise.

AI.tldr: The paper studies nonequilibrium dynamics after a quantum quench in spin chains solvable by mapping to free fermions in disguise, where all energy eigenvalues are exponentially degenerate. The authors develop an analytic method to compute the quasi-momentum distribution for the generalized Gibbs ensemble and derive analytic formulas for expectation values of special observables. They also propose a modified formula for entanglement growth based on the quasi-particle picture, accounting for extra entropy from the exponential degeneracy. Numerical tensor-network computations show excellent agreement for local observables and small deviations for entanglement dynamics.
AI.motivation: To understand whether the established framework for out-of-equilibrium integrable systems remains valid in models where free fermions in disguise exhibit exponential degeneracy of all energy eigenvalues.
AI.method: Analytic method to compute quasi-momentum distribution for the generalized Gibbs ensemble; analytic formula for expectation values of special observables; modified quasi-particle picture for entanglement entropy growth; numerical tensor-network computations for verification.
AI.result: Excellent agreement between theoretical predictions and numerical simulations for local observables; small deviations for entanglement dynamics, indicating the conjecture is only approximately correct.
AI.conclusion: This work is a first step toward extending the established framework of integrable systems out of equilibrium to models hosting free fermions in disguise.

title: Phonon spectral function of Holstein polaron: Investigation of many-body effects with self-energy and vertex correction
summary: We study the impact of the many-body effects on the phonon spectral function of Holstein polaron in one-dimension in the antiadiabatic regime by incorporating the contributions from the electron self-energy and vertex corrections within a weak-coupling approach that respects the charge-conserving Ward identity. We find that while the polaronic spectral weight is suppressed due to contribution from the electron self-energy, on the other hand, the same is enhanced due to contribution from the vertex corrections. While strength of both the contributions increases with increasing the wave vector ($\q$) of phonons, they nearly cancel each other for the small-$\q$ modes so that the polaronic spectral weight is weakly affected due to the many-body effects. For the large-$\q$ modes near the zone boundary, the net many-body correction is dominated by the contribution of the electron self-energy which increases faster in comparison to that of the vertex corrections with increasing the wave vector thereby resulting in a significant suppression of the polaronic spectral weight. We find that while the weak-coupling perturbative approach provides a reliable estimation of the impact of the many-body effects deep inside the antiadibatic regime, the renormalization of quasiparticle spectrum must be taken into account for an accurate estimation when the phonon energy approaches the electronic bandwidth.

AI.tldr: The paper studies many-body effects on the phonon spectral function of the Holstein polaron in 1D in the antiadiabatic regime, finding that electron self-energy suppresses while vertex corrections enhance polaronic spectral weight, with near-cancellation for small-q modes but net suppression for large-q modes near the zone boundary.
AI.motivation: To investigate the impact of many-body effects (electron self-energy and vertex corrections) on the phonon spectral function of the Holstein polaron in the antiadiabatic regime, using a charge-conserving weak-coupling approach.
AI.method: A weak-coupling perturbative approach that respects the charge-conserving Ward identity, incorporating both electron self-energy and vertex corrections in one-dimensional Holstein model.
AI.result: Electron self-energy suppresses polaronic spectral weight while vertex corrections enhance it. For small-q modes, these contributions nearly cancel. For large-q modes near the zone boundary, net many-body correction is dominated by electron self-energy, causing significant suppression of spectral weight.
AI.conclusion: The weak-coupling approach is reliable deep in the antiadiabatic regime, but renormalization of the quasiparticle spectrum must be accounted for when phonon energy approaches the electronic bandwidth.

title: Quantifying angular momentum of coherently driven circular phonons
summary: The use of intense terahertz (THz) pulses to manipulate low-energy excitations offers a powerful approach for ultrafast control of electronic and magnetic properties in materials. Theory suggests that circular ionic motions driven by THz fields carry angular momentum, potentially generating internal magnetic fields. Recent experiments in nonmagnetic SrTiO3 (STO) have hinted at such THz-induced fields, but their origin remains debated. Here, we employ ultrafast x-ray diffraction to resolve the time-dependent ionic trajectories in STO following excitation by circularly polarized THz pulses. Our analysis reveals that oxygen ions, despite their lower mass, contribute around 90% of the phonon angular momentum. The resulting imbalance between the negatively and positively charged ions provides a clear explanation for the mechanism behind induced magnetism in STO. This work further provides the first quantitative measurement of circular ionic motions and their angular momentum and establishes a general methodology for the investigation of angular momentum transfer in solids, paving the way for new strategies to control topological phonon transport and phonon-driven magnetism in quantum materials.

AI.tldr: Using ultrafast x-ray diffraction, the authors show that circularly polarized THz pulses drive oxygen ions (contributing ~90% of phonon angular momentum) in SrTiO3, creating a charge imbalance that explains the induced magnetism, and provide the first quantitative measurement of circular ionic motions and their angular momentum.
AI.motivation: To resolve the debated origin of THz-induced internal magnetic fields in nonmagnetic SrTiO3 by directly measuring time-dependent ionic trajectories and phonon angular momentum contributions.
AI.method: Ultrafast x-ray diffraction was employed to resolve time-dependent ionic trajectories in SrTiO3 following excitation by circularly polarized THz pulses.
AI.result: Oxygen ions contribute ~90% of the phonon angular momentum despite their lower mass; the charge imbalance between negative and positive ions explains the mechanism of THz-induced magnetism in SrTiO3.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first quantitative measurement of circular ionic motions and their angular momentum, establishing a general methodology for studying angular momentum transfer in solids and enabling new strategies for controlling topological phonon transport and phonon-driven magnetism in quantum materials.

title: Entropy of Non-Abelian Anyons from Slow Quasiparticle Dynamics in Quantum Hall Interferometers
summary: Non-Abelian anyons emerging in fractional quantum Hall states carry a characteristic entropy, $ΔS = k_B \log d$, where \(d\) is the anyon's quantum dimension. This \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) entropy can, in principle, be extracted from charge measurements of an antidot via Maxwell relations. However, equilibrium charge measurements in fractional antidots have proven to be challenging with conventional charge detectors. Here, we propose a scheme based on an antidot embedded in an interferometer, in which the charge can be inferred from the recently observed time-dependent switching of the interference phase. Performing such non-local charge measurements at equilibrium, the characteristic \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) entropy of non-Abelian anyons (e.g., $d = \sqrt{2}$ for the $ν= 5/2$ state) can be extracted for intermediate temperatures, which exceed the level spacing of the interferometer edge, but are much smaller than the level spacing of the antidot.

AI.tldr: A scheme to extract the characteristic O(1) entropy of non-Abelian anyons (e.g., d=√2 for ν=5/2) using an antidot embedded in an interferometer, where charge is inferred from time-dependent switching of the interference phase, enabling non-local equilibrium charge measurements at intermediate temperatures.
AI.motivation: Non-Abelian anyons in fractional quantum Hall states carry a characteristic entropy ΔS = k_B log d, but equilibrium charge measurements in fractional antidots with conventional charge detectors have proven challenging.
AI.method: Proposes an antidot embedded in an interferometer, where charge is inferred from time-dependent switching of the interference phase, enabling non-local equilibrium charge measurements.
AI.result: The characteristic O(1) entropy of non-Abelian anyons (e.g., d = √2 for the ν = 5/2 state) can be extracted for intermediate temperatures that exceed the level spacing of the interferometer edge but are much smaller than the level spacing of the antidot.
AI.conclusion: Non-local charge measurements via interferometry provide a viable route to detect non-Abelian anyon entropy, overcoming the limitations of conventional charge detectors.

title: A density matrix renormalization group approach to quantum point contacts
summary: Using the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) combined with the correction-vector method, we investigate the competition between an harmonic potential and repulsive interactions in a one-dimensional fermionic system. The parabolic confinement induces spatial inhomogeneity, and by tuning its curvature one can continuously interpolate between a potential well--relevant for cold-atom setups--and a quantum barrier, as realized in mesoscopic systems such as quantum point contacts. We analyze how the ground-state particle distribution evolves with the strength and sign of the confining potential and how the confinement reshapes the spectral weight of the local density of states (LDOS) at the center of the chain. In the barrier regime, a localized peak emerges in the electron part of the spectrum ($ω>0$) as a direct consequence of the potential. In contrast, in the well configuration and for weak interactions, a localized feature persists but shifts to the hole sector ($ω<0$). However, for stronger interactions, the LDOS no longer displays clear signatures of the external potential, indicating that correlations dominate over single-particle confinement.

AI.tldr: Using DMRG with correction-vector method, this paper studies how a 1D fermionic system responds to harmonic confinement (from well to barrier) and repulsive interactions, showing that the local density of states exhibits potential-induced spectral features that are suppressed by strong correlations.
AI.motivation: To understand the competition between external confinement (harmonic potential) and repulsive interactions in one-dimensional fermionic systems, bridging cold-atom setups (potential well) and mesoscopic systems like quantum point contacts (potential barrier).
AI.method: Density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) combined with the correction-vector method.
AI.result: In the barrier regime, a localized peak appears in the electron sector (ω>0); in the well regime with weak interactions, a localized feature shifts to the hole sector (ω<0); for strong interactions, LDOS shows no clear potential-induced features.
AI.conclusion: Correlations dominate over single-particle confinement at strong interactions, suppressing spectral signatures of the external potential.

title: HVAF Spraying of NiTi Coatings: Microstructure, Phase Transformation and Shape Memory Behavior
summary: Depositing various coatings on surface of engineering components with the aim to improve their performance concerning wear, corrosion, friction and thermal protection is already a standard practice. Depositing metallic NiTi shape memory alloy coatings may be a viable alternative for hard ceramic coatings. NiTi coatings offer additional benefits originating from unique functional thermomechanical properties. However, fabrication of thick NiTi coatings turned out to be difficult. Standard electroplating and laser cladding methods are not suitable for NiTi the most widely used plasma spray methods tend to produce chemically inhomogeneous coatings that do not transform martensitically, cold sprayed NiTi coatings suffer from poor adhesion to the substrates. In this work we report on first ever successful fabrication of thick NiTi coatings (100-300 um) that display functional thermomechanical properties and simultaneously show very good adherence to the substrate. We used high velocity air fuel thermal spray method to fabricate NiTi coatings deposited on mild steel using four different sets of processing parameters. Chemical composition, porosity, microstructure, phase transformation and functional thermomechanical properties of the NiTi coatings were evaluated. Although the coatings contain inhomogeneous microstructure, voids, oxide particles, high density of dislocation defects and internal stress, they undergo martensitic transformation upon cooling and or mechanical loading. As sprayed NiTi coatings need to be annealed to display functional thermomechanical properties. Despite their limited tensile strength, the coatings displayed thermal actuation in 3 point bending tests and shape memory effects in nanoindentation and scratch tests.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the first successful fabrication of thick NiTi shape memory alloy coatings (100-300 μm) on mild steel using high velocity air fuel (HVAF) thermal spraying, which exhibit martensitic transformation, good adhesion, and functional thermomechanical properties after annealing, overcoming limitations of prior methods like plasma spray, cold spray, electroplating, and laser cladding.
AI.motivation: To fabricate thick NiTi shape memory alloy coatings with functional thermomechanical properties (shape memory effect, thermal actuation) and good substrate adhesion, addressing the difficulties encountered with conventional methods such as electroplating, laser cladding, plasma spray, and cold spray.
AI.method: High velocity air fuel (HVAF) thermal spray method was used to deposit NiTi coatings (100-300 μm) on mild steel with four different processing parameter sets. Coatings were characterized for chemical composition, porosity, microstructure, phase transformations, and functional properties. Post-deposition annealing was applied to enable thermomechanical functionality.
AI.result: The coatings, despite containing inhomogeneous microstructure, voids, oxide particles, dislocations, and internal stress, undergo martensitic transformation upon cooling or mechanical loading. Annealing is required to display functional thermomechanical properties. Coatings show thermal actuation in 3-point bending tests and shape memory effects in nanoindentation and scratch tests, though tensile strength is limited.
AI.conclusion: HVAF thermal spraying enables successful fabrication of thick, well-adhered NiTi coatings with functional shape memory and actuation properties, offering a viable alternative to hard ceramic coatings for wear, corrosion, friction, and thermal protection applications.

title: Josephson and Spin Currents in Coupled Polariton Condensates
summary: We analyze particle and spin currents in networks of coupled spinor exciton-polariton condensates arranged as plaquettes and regular polygonal rings. In closed geometries, spin-conserving and TE-TM-induced spin-flip tunnelling combine to generate circulating particle currents, hidden spin counterflows, and bond-dependent spin-current patterns. For the minimal geometries - an equilateral triangle, and a square plaquette - we derive analytical expressions for edge-resolved currents from stationary configurations obtained by energy minimization. We then show how particle, in-plane spin, and out-of-plane spin currents partition the parameter plane and provide direct signatures of the equilibrium phases. Finally, we apply the same current-resolved diagnostics to larger rings, where winding numbers and a branch-invariant common-phase coherence metric organize the resulting phase structure.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes particle and spin currents in coupled spinor exciton-polariton condensates arranged in plaquettes and polygonal rings, deriving analytical expressions for edge-resolved currents in minimal geometries (triangle, square), mapping current patterns to equilibrium phases, and extending diagnostics to larger rings with winding-number-based phase organization.
AI.motivation: To understand how spin-conserving and TE-TM-induced spin-flip tunnelling generate circulating particle currents, hidden spin counterflows, and bond-dependent spin-current patterns in geometrically confined polariton condensate networks.
AI.method: Analytical derivation of edge-resolved current expressions from energy-minimized stationary configurations for minimal geometries (equilateral triangle and square plaquette), followed by parameter-plane partitioning using particle, in-plane spin, and out-of-plane spin currents; application of current-resolved diagnostics to larger rings with winding numbers and common-phase coherence metrics.
AI.result: Analytical formulas for edge-resolved currents in triangle and square geometries; demonstration that particle and spin currents provide direct signatures of equilibrium phases; successful organization of phase structure in larger rings using winding numbers and a branch-invariant common-phase coherence metric.
AI.conclusion: Current-resolved diagnostics serve as effective tools for characterizing equilibrium phases in spinor polariton networks, with the framework extendable to larger ring geometries where winding-number and coherence metrics capture the phase organization.

title: Fundamental limitations of single-particle Green's-function zeroes as probes of many-body topology
summary: We show that topological invariants constructed from single-particle Green's functions (GFs) cannot reliably diagnose the topology of interacting many-body states. Using coupled interacting SSH chains as a minimal example, we demonstrate that a spin-spin interaction can trivialize the many-body ground state without affecting the GF topological invariant. This breakdown originates from the GF's inability to probe electronic excitations in the Fock sectors responsible for the topological degeneracy. Consequently, GF zeroes are not associated with physical topological quasiparticles and cannot generally characterize interacting topological phases.

AI.tldr: Topological invariants from single-particle Green's functions fail to diagnose topology of interacting many-body states, as shown in coupled SSH chains where interaction trivializes the ground state without affecting the GF invariant. GF zeroes are not linked to physical topological quasiparticles.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that topological invariants computed from single-particle Green's functions are unreliable for diagnosing the topology of interacting many-body systems, and to identify the fundamental reason for this breakdown.
AI.method: Using coupled interacting SSH (Su-Schrieffer-Heeger) chains as a minimal model, the authors analyze how a spin-spin interaction affects the many-body ground state topology and compare it with the behavior of Green's function topological invariants.
AI.result: A spin-spin interaction can trivialize the many-body ground state while leaving the GF topological invariant unchanged. Green's functions fail to probe electronic excitations in Fock sectors responsible for topological degeneracy.
AI.conclusion: GF zeroes are not associated with physical topological quasiparticles and cannot generally characterize interacting topological phases, indicating a fundamental limitation of single-particle Green's functions in diagnosing interacting topology.

title: Transition-Metal Tailored $Ga_{2}O_{2}$ Monolayer: From Room-Temperature Gas Sensing to Chemical Scavenging
summary: Pristine $Ga_{2}O_{2}$ monolayers suffer from poor sensitivity and weak molecular capture, limiting their application in toxic gas detection and environmental detoxification. Here, we employ first-principles density functional theory (DFT) calculations to investigate the gas sensing and scavenging properties of $Ga_{2}O_{2}$ monolayers substitutionally tailored via seven transition-metals (TM): Pd, Zn, Zr, Mo, Ag, Ti, and Pt. All TM-substituted monolayers exhibit negative formation and binding energies, negligible lattice distortion, and structural stability in molecular dynamics simulations. Performance evaluation against eight toxic industrial and three environmental gases reveals functionalities ranging from selective, reusable room-temperature sensing to permanent molecular capture. Ag substitution exhibits exceptional selectivity for $NO$ with moderate adsorption strength (~-0.83eV), an up to eight-order-of-magnitude conductivity enhancement, besides facilitating reusable $O_2$ and $NO_2$ detection. Additionally, Pd-, Zn-, Zr-, and Mo substitutions tune selectivity toward $NO$, $NO_2$, $CO_2$, $CO$, and $O_2$. Coming to applications towards toxic gas capture, Zr- and Mo-substituted systems selectively scavenge oxidizing gases, whereas Ti and Pt act as universal scavengers. Further analysis reveals that Pd- and Ag-substituted monolayers remain selective for $NO$, while Zn substitution favors $NO_2$ detection even in ambient atmospheric conditions. Thus, these tailored $Ga_{2}O_{2}$ monolayers offer a practical platform for atmospheric monitoring and detoxification.

AI.tldr: First-principles DFT study shows TM-substituted Ga₂O₂ monolayers (Pd, Zn, Zr, Mo, Ag, Ti, Pt) exhibit tunable gas sensing and scavenging properties, with Ag offering selective NO detection and Ti/Pt acting as universal toxic gas scavengers.
AI.motivation: Pristine Ga₂O₂ monolayers suffer from poor sensitivity and weak molecular capture, limiting applications in toxic gas detection and environmental detoxification, motivating the exploration of transition-metal substitutional tailoring.
AI.method: First-principles DFT calculations were performed on Ga₂O₂ monolayers substitutionally tailored with seven transition metals (Pd, Zn, Zr, Mo, Ag, Ti, Pt) to evaluate their gas sensing and scavenging properties against eight toxic industrial and three environmental gases.
AI.result: All TM-substituted monolayers show negative formation/binding energies, negligible lattice distortion, and structural stability. Ag substitution provides exceptional NO selectivity (~-0.83eV), eight-order conductivity enhancement, and reusable O₂/NO₂ detection. Pd, Zn, Zr, Mo tune selectivity toward NO, NO₂, CO₂, CO, O₂. Zr/Mo selectively scavenge oxidizing gases; Ti/Pt act as universal scavengers.
AI.conclusion: TM-tailored Ga₂O₂ monolayers offer a practical platform for atmospheric monitoring and detoxification, with tunable selectivity for specific toxic gases and capabilities ranging from reusable sensing to permanent molecular capture.

title: Coupled Spin-Orbital $p$-Wave Magnetism via Structural and Magnetic Chirality
summary: Helical spin textures represent the minimal realization of $p$-wave magnetism which is characterized by momentum-odd spin polarization. Independently, structurally chiral crystals exhibit momentum-odd orbital polarization arising from broken inversion symmetry. Here, we demonstrate that spin-orbit coupling couples these two independent microscopic chirality degrees of freedom, allowing the orbital polarization of a chiral crystal to generate an additional contribution to the $p$-wave spin splitting. The resulting spin-orbital state is naturally classified by the relative chirality $η=χ_{\mathrm c}χ_{\mathrm m}$, giving rise to two symmetry-distinct $p$-wave phases corresponding to homochiral and heterochiral configurations which can be directly probed by the longitudinal conductivity. These phases exhibit distinct transport signatures, establishing relative chirality as an experimentally accessible symmetry degree of freedom in chiral magnetic systems.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that spin-orbit coupling links structural chirality and magnetic helicity in crystals, creating two distinct p-wave phases (homochiral/heterochiral) with different conductivity signatures, defining relative chirality as a new symmetry degree of freedom.
AI.motivation: To understand how spin-orbit coupling couples the microscopic chirality of structural chirality (orbital polarization) and helical magnetism (spin polarization), and to classify the resulting spin-orbital states.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis using spin-orbit coupling to couple structural chirality (momentum-odd orbital polarization) and helical magnetism (momentum-odd spin polarization), classifying p-wave phases by relative chirality η = χ_c χ_m.
AI.result: Two symmetry-distinct p-wave phases emerge: homochiral and heterochiral configurations, distinguishable by longitudinal conductivity measurements.
AI.conclusion: Relative chirality is an experimentally accessible symmetry degree of freedom in chiral magnetic systems, with distinct transport signatures.

title: Anomalous thermopower from the drag of overdamped collective modes
summary: Inspired by the observation of a Seebeck coefficient ratio that exhibits a seemingly logarithmic divergence at low temperature in high-temperature superconducting cuprates, we show that a mechanisms similar to the standard phonon drag can give rise to anomalies in the thermopower of a metal, if the dragged collective mode is overdamped, with a damping coefficient that increases with lowering the temperature. Our finding adds a piece to the puzzle of the strange-metal behavior observed in many different systems and supports our proposal that overdamped charge density fluctuations can be responsible of such a behavior in high-temperature superconducting cuprates.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that an overdamped collective mode (like charge density fluctuations) with temperature-dependent damping can cause anomalous thermopower behavior in strange metals, explaining the logarithmic divergence of the Seebeck coefficient ratio observed in high-temperature superconducting cuprates.
AI.motivation: To explain the puzzling logarithmic divergence of the Seebeck coefficient ratio observed at low temperatures in high-temperature superconducting cuprates, which is a signature of strange-metal behavior.
AI.method: The authors extend the standard phonon drag mechanism to the case of an overdamped collective mode, where the damping coefficient increases with decreasing temperature, and show how this produces anomalies in thermopower.
AI.result: A mechanism analogous to phonon drag, but applied to overdamped collective modes (e.g., charge density fluctuations), can reproduce the anomalous thermopower behavior and the seemingly logarithmic divergence of the Seebeck coefficient ratio at low temperatures.
AI.conclusion: Overdamped charge density fluctuations with temperature-dependent damping are a plausible microscopic origin of the strange-metal thermopower anomaly in high-temperature superconducting cuprates, adding insight into the broader strange-metal phenomenology.

title: A depth resolved investigation of hydrogen uptake in carbon based nanostructures by soft-to-hard photoemission spectroscopy
summary: Hydrogen chemisorption on graphitic carbon modifies the carbon orbital hybridization from sp2 to sp3, altering both structural and electronic properties. Understanding not only the lateral extent but also the depth distribution of hydrogen uptake in three-dimensional carbon architectures is essential for both fundamental studies and storage applications. To this end, we investigate here the evolution of the C 1s core-level lineshape in nanoporous graphene (NPG) and vertically aligned carbon nanotubes (CNTs) upon hydrogenation, exploiting soft-to-hard X-ray photoemission spectroscopy to achieve a depth-resolved analysis. Decomposition of the C 1s spectra reveals the formation of an sp3 rich overlayer in both systems, with an effective thickness ranging from a fraction of a graphitic monolayer (NPG) to approximately one graphitic layer (CNTs), indicating limited hydrogen penetration beneath the outermost accessible surfaces. Overall, hydrogenation in both materials remains predominantly localized on the surface. These results clarify the spatial distribution of hydrogen in curved and porous graphitic networks and provide quantitative constraints on its chemisorption for carbon-based hydrogen storage applications.

AI.tldr: Using depth-resolved X-ray photoemission spectroscopy, the study shows that hydrogen chemisorption on nanoporous graphene and carbon nanotubes is limited to surface layers (0.5-1 monolayer), forming an sp³-rich overlayer with minimal subsurface penetration.
AI.motivation: To understand both the lateral extent and depth distribution of hydrogen uptake in three-dimensional carbon architectures, which is essential for fundamental studies and hydrogen storage applications.
AI.method: Soft-to-hard X-ray photoemission spectroscopy (XPS) depth-resolved analysis of C 1s core-level lineshapes in nanoporous graphene (NPG) and vertically aligned carbon nanotubes (CNTs) upon hydrogenation.
AI.result: Decomposition of C 1s spectra reveals an sp³-rich overlayer with effective thickness ranging from a fraction of a graphitic monolayer (NPG) to approximately one graphitic layer (CNTs), indicating limited hydrogen penetration.
AI.conclusion: Hydrogenation remains predominantly surface-localized in both curved and porous graphitic networks, providing quantitative constraints for carbon-based hydrogen storage applications.

title: Intrinsic orbital Hall effect in a nonuniform electric field
summary: Geometric analysis of electronic Bloch states offers a universal framework for understanding electronic properties, yet its role in the transport of orbital angular momentum remains unexplored. In this work, we establish an analytic connection between orbital angular momentum transport and the geometric properties of Bloch wave functions in electronic systems. Focusing on the intrinsic orbital Hall effect in the dc limit under a spatially nonuniform electric field, we show that its conductivity can be expressed in terms of universal geometric quantities, such as the orbital Berry curvature and quantum metric. This formulation provides a term-by-term correspondence with the geometric description of intrinsic charge Hall transport established in previous studies. Using a tight-binding model, we further illustrate that the higher-order orbital Hall response can exhibit enhanced sensitivity to the orientation of an anisotropic sample. Our work deepens the understanding of diverse intrinsic transverse transport phenomena and the role of quantum geometry in electronic systems.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes an analytic connection between orbital angular momentum transport and the geometric properties (orbital Berry curvature and quantum metric) of Bloch wave functions, showing that orbital Hall conductivity in the dc limit under nonuniform electric fields can be expressed using universal geometric quantities.
AI.motivation: While geometric analysis of Bloch states is well-established for electronic properties, its role in orbital angular momentum transport was unexplored.
AI.method: Analytic derivation connecting orbital Hall conductivity to orbital Berry curvature and quantum metric; tight-binding model illustration of higher-order orbital Hall response anisotropy.
AI.result: Orbital Hall conductivity in the dc limit under nonuniform electric fields can be expressed via universal geometric quantities (orbital Berry curvature and quantum metric), with term-by-term correspondence to geometric description of charge Hall transport.
AI.conclusion: Deepens understanding of intrinsic transverse transport phenomena and the role of quantum geometry in electronic systems; higher-order orbital Hall response shows enhanced sensitivity to sample orientation.

title: Anisotropic nanoscale coherent polariton transport in CrSBr
summary: In a combined experimental and theoretical study, we demonstrate anisotropic polariton transport on the nanoscale in the van der Waals antiferromagnet CrSBr. While effective cavity-polariton formation emerges via the self-hybridization of ultra-high oscillator strength excitons with a thin slab photonic mode, the absence of external mirrors facilitates spectroscopic investigation of these polaritons via cathodoluminescence (CL) on length scales determined by the electron wavelength. This direct access allows us to perform precise charting of the polariton landscape with nanometric resolution, and to probe polariton interference phenomena. The main finding of the work highlights that the coherent polariton transport follows the $C_{2v}$ symmetry of CrSBr, allowing exclusive transport along the crystallographic a-axis, while no coherent feature is found along the b-axis direction. Our work sets the foundation to use CL spectroscopy in cavity-polaritonics in more advanced landscapes, such as photonic crystals or optical lattices, and establishes the technique as a powerful tool to probe anisotropic expansion and relaxation phenomena on the nanoscale

AI.tldr: Using cathodoluminescence spectroscopy, researchers demonstrate anisotropic nanoscale polariton transport in the van der Waals antiferromagnet CrSBr, where polaritons propagate coherently only along the crystallographic a-axis (C2v symmetry), with no coherent transport along the b-axis.
AI.motivation: To investigate nanoscale polariton transport in cavity-free systems by leveraging self-hybridized exciton-photonic modes in CrSBr, and to establish cathodoluminescence as a tool for probing polariton dynamics with nanometer spatial resolution.
AI.method: Combined experimental and theoretical study using cathodoluminescence (CL) spectroscopy to probe self-hybridized cavity-polaritons formed from ultra-high oscillator strength excitons coupled to thin slab photonic modes in CrSBr, without external mirrors.
AI.result: Polariton transport follows C2v symmetry of CrSBr, with coherent transport exclusively along the crystallographic a-axis; no coherent features observed along the b-axis. Nanometric-resolution mapping of the polariton landscape and polariton interference phenomena were achieved.
AI.conclusion: CL spectroscopy is established as a powerful tool for cavity-polaritonics in complex landscapes (photonic crystals, optical lattices) and for probing anisotropic nanoscale expansion and relaxation phenomena.

title: Coherent two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy integrated with confocal back focal plane microscopy
summary: We introduce a setup for coherent two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy in the pump-probe reflection geometry that is integrated with a confocal back focal plane imaging microscope. The angle-resolved capability is utilized to control pump and probe wavevectors, while real space imaging enables co-localization of the collection spots for linear and ultrafast experiments. Compression of pulses down to 20 fs is achieved. We demonstrate the capabilities of this approach on an exfoliated WSe$_2$ monolayer on Si/SiO$_2$. The setup is suited to investigate excitons and exciton-polaritons in 2D Materials and their heterostructures.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a setup for coherent 2D electronic spectroscopy in pump-probe reflection geometry, integrated with a confocal back focal plane imaging microscope, enabling angle-resolved and real-space imaging capabilities for studying excitons and exciton-polaritons in 2D materials, demonstrated on a WSe₂ monolayer.
AI.motivation: To develop an advanced spectroscopic setup that combines coherent two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy with reflection geometry and microscopy for investigating excitons and exciton-polaritons in 2D materials and heterostructures.
AI.method: Coherent two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy in pump-probe reflection geometry integrated with a confocal back focal plane imaging microscope, featuring angle-resolved wavevector control, real-space imaging co-localization, and pulse compression down to 20 fs.
AI.result: Demonstrated capabilities on an exfoliated WSe₂ monolayer on Si/SiO₂ substrate, achieving 20 fs pulse compression and combined angle-resolved and real-space imaging for ultrafast experiments.
AI.conclusion: The setup is well-suited for investigating excitons and exciton-polaritons in 2D Materials and their heterostructures.

title: From Bloch to Néel: Anisotropy-dependent Domain-Wall Character in FePd Thin Films
summary: We report an experimental investigation of the depth-dependent domain wall formation in L1$_0$-FePd thin films with high perpendicular magnetic anisotropy. Using circular dichroism X-ray resonant magnetic scattering (CD-XRMS) as a function of the incident X-ray angle, we explore the depth evolution of chiral spin textures in two samples with different strengths of magnetocrystalline anisotropy. Combined with CD-STXM, CD-ptychography, and macroscopic characterization of the structural order, magnetic properties, and surface morphology, we relate these observations to differences in the long-range order of the L1$_0$ phase of FePd. One FePd thin film with very high magnetocrystalline anisotropy, characterized by $Q_{PMA}=1.8$, exhibits an unexpectedly large Néel contribution. Angular-dependent CD-XRMS directly reveals a smooth transition from a hybrid Bloch-Néel chirality within the upper FePd layer towards a purely Néel-type structure at the lower FePd interface. In the second FePd sample, despite a still relatively large $Q_{PMA}=1.45$, the domain walls were found to be purely Néel type. These results indicate a crucial role of the long-range structural order in determining the formation of the magnetic structure.

AI.tldr: CD-XRMS and other X-ray techniques reveal depth-dependent domain wall chirality transitions (Bloch-Néel hybrid to pure Néel) in L1₀-FePd thin films, strongly influenced by long-range structural order and magnetocrystalline anisotropy strength.
AI.motivation: To understand the depth evolution of chiral spin textures in L1₀-FePd thin films with high perpendicular magnetic anisotropy, and how magnetocrystalline anisotropy strength and long-range structural order affect domain wall formation.
AI.method: Circular dichroism X-ray resonant magnetic scattering (CD-XRMS) as a function of incident X-ray angle, combined with CD-STXM, CD-ptychography, and macroscopic characterization of structural order, magnetic properties, and surface morphology.
AI.result: High-anisotropy sample (QPMA=1.8) shows unexpectedly large Néel contribution with smooth transition from hybrid Bloch-Néel at upper layer to pure Néel at lower interface. Moderate-anisotropy sample (QPMA=1.45) exhibits purely Néel-type domain walls.
AI.conclusion: Long-range structural order plays a crucial role in determining magnetic structure formation, including domain wall chirality, in L1₀-FePd thin films.

title: Ultrafast Demagnetization Governed by Spin Fluctuations in CaRuO$_{3}$/SrTiO$_{3}$ Superlattice
summary: For ultrafast magnetization switching devices, critical slowing down in conventional ferromagnets near their Curie temperature constitutes a key challenge that must be overcome. In contrast to this typical behavior, we observe an anomalous acceleration of demagnetization in CaRuO$_{3}$/SrTiO$_{3}$ superlattices, a moderately correlated weak itinerant ferromagnet. The demagnetization rate increases with rising temperature, pump fluence, and applied magnetic field. To explain these anomalous phenomena, we develop a phenomenological model integrating the three-temperature model with self-consistent renormalization theory. Because the intrinsic gradient magnetism of the superlattice suppresses the typical divergence of specific heat, the conventional thermodynamic bottleneck is bypassed. Our model reveals that this decoupling enables the ultrafast dynamics to be predominantly governed by the spin-fluctuation-driven enhancement of the electron-spin scattering vertex. Our work demonstrates how spatial inhomogeneity can decouple macroscopic thermodynamic singularities from microscopic scattering processes, offering a new paradigm for manipulating ultrafast spin dynamics in correlated quantum materials. The pronounced sensitivity of the demagnetization rate to external parameters further suggests the potential for designing highly tunable ultrafast spintronic devices that leverage enhanced fluctuations near the magnetic instability.

AI.tldr: CaRuO₃/SrTiO₃ superlattices exhibit anomalous acceleration (rather than slowing down) of ultrafast demagnetization with increasing temperature, fluence, and magnetic field. This arises from spatial inhomogeneity decoupling thermodynamic singularities from microscopic scattering, governed by spin-fluctuation-enhanced electron-spin scattering.
AI.motivation: Conventional ferromagnets suffer from critical slowing down near the Curie temperature, which hinders ultrafast magnetization switching. The authors aim to overcome this thermodynamic bottleneck by exploring correlated materials with spatial inhomogeneity.
AI.method: Femtosecond pump-probe spectroscopy on CaRuO₃/SrTiO₃ superlattices; phenomenological model integrating the three-temperature model with self-consistent renormalization (SCR) theory.
AI.result: Demagnetization rate accelerates with rising temperature, pump fluence, and applied magnetic field—opposite to conventional ferromagnets. The intrinsic gradient magnetism suppresses specific heat divergence, removing the thermodynamic bottleneck.
AI.conclusion: Spatial inhomogeneity can decouple macroscopic thermodynamic singularities from microscopic scattering processes, enabling a new paradigm for designing tunable ultrafast spintronic devices via enhanced fluctuations near magnetic instability.

title: Interfacial Strain and Structural Defects Govern the Performance of Tantalum Superconducting Waveguide Resonators
summary: Tantalum (Ta) is a promising material for reaching long coherence times in superconducting qubits. A detailed understanding of the underlying structure-property relationship remains elusive though. In the present study, we sputter-deposited 200 nm thick Ta films on high-resistivity silicon (100) substrates at temperatures ranging from T = 20°C to 600°C, as well as on different seed layers (Nb, TiN and TaN). Alpha-Ta thin films were readily obtained at temperatures above 500°C and on all seed layers. The films were characterized in terms of surface morphology, residual-resistance ratio, crystal phase composition and superconducting transition temperature, as well as RF-performance using coplanar waveguide resonators. Internal quality factors of up to 1.5 million were measured at 100 mK in the single-photon regime. Despite similar bulk material properties, alpha-Ta films on different seed layers exhibit markedly different RF-performance, which we attribute to dissimilar strain and structural defects at the substrate-metal interfaces. Williamson-Hall analysis of XRD data reveals a clear correlation between decreasing microstrain and increasing quality factor. Cross-sectional HR-TEM further supports this interpretation by directly resolving interfacial disorder. Our results highlight the critical role of interface engineering in optimizing superconducting thin films for low-loss quantum computing circuitry.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how sputter-deposited alpha-Ta thin films on various substrates and seed layers affect superconducting qubit performance, finding that interfacial strain and structural defects at the substrate-metal interface—rather than bulk material properties—are the key determinants of RF-performance, with internal quality factors reaching up to 1.5 million.
AI.motivation: Tantalum shows promise for long coherence times in superconducting qubits, but the structure-property relationship underlying its performance remains poorly understood, motivating a systematic study of how deposition conditions and interfaces affect film quality and RF behavior.
AI.method: 200 nm thick Ta films were sputter-deposited on high-resistivity Si(100) substrates at 20–600°C and on Nb, TiN, and TaN seed layers. Films were characterized by surface morphology, residual-resistance ratio, XRD phase composition, superconducting transition temperature, and RF-performance using coplanar waveguide resonators. Williamson-Hall analysis and cross-sectional HR-TEM were used to correlate microstrain and interfacial disorder with quality factor.
AI.result: Alpha-Ta films were obtained above 500°C and on all seed layers. Internal quality factors up to 1.5 million were measured at 100 mK in the single-photon regime. Despite similar bulk properties, alpha-Ta on different seed layers showed markedly different RF-performance. Williamson-Hall analysis revealed a clear correlation between decreasing microstrain and increasing quality factor, and HR-TEM directly resolved interfacial disorder.
AI.conclusion: Interface engineering—specifically controlling strain and structural defects at the substrate-metal interface—is critical for optimizing superconducting thin films for low-loss quantum computing circuitry, rather than focusing solely on bulk material properties.

title: Bottlenecks in Hamiltonian-Adaptive Resolution Simulation Method for Modeling Interfaces
summary: The Hamiltonian-Adaptive Resolution Simulation (H-AdResS) method allows to combine atomistic and particle-based coarse-grained models in a single simulation box, which makes it very attractive to model systems containing interfaces or reactive regions surrounded by an interacting environment. In our previous work [arXiv:2604.21867], we implemented H-AdResS in LAMMPS 2023 and extended its use to interfaces, focusing on MOF/CO$_2$ interfaces as an example. We found that, despite its advantages, using this method properly for this kind of systems is not trivial. In this work, an in-depth analysis of the impact of the choice of thermostatting schemes and long-range electrostatics models is presented. Even though its Hamiltonian formulation enables performing H-AdResS simulations within constant temperatures ensembles, not every thermostat is appropriate. We demonstrate that Langevin thermostat is a reliable choice for this method, while Nosé-Hoover results in artifacts. In addition, we show that using short-range models such as the Damped Shifted Force method for electrostatics, a popular choice for H-AdResS simulations, can lead to non-physical results when modeling interfaces. The need of capping strategies to deal with discontinuities in forces and energies arising from abrupt changes in resolution is also discussed. Finally, the impossibility of changing the definition of the H-AdResS Hamiltonian to include a gradual interpolation of the bonded degrees of freedom is discussed. We hope that this contribution helps the reader to appropriately set up H-AdResS simulations and to assess if this method can be used to accurately model their system of interest.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the impact of thermostatting schemes and long-range electrostatic models on H-AdResS simulations in LAMMPS, finding that Langevin thermostat is reliable while Nosé-Hoover causes artifacts, and that short-range electrostatic models can produce non-physical results at interfaces.
AI.motivation: To provide guidance on proper setup of H-AdResS simulations for systems with interfaces (e.g., MOF/CO₂), as using this method correctly is non-trivial despite its advantages.
AI.method: In-depth analysis of thermostatting schemes (Langevin vs. Nosé-Hoover) and long-range electrostatics models (including Damped Shifted Force method) in H-AdResS simulations implemented in LAMMPS, with discussion of capping strategies for force/energy discontinuities and bonded degree of freedom interpolation limitations.
AI.result: Langevin thermostat is reliable; Nosé-Hoover introduces artifacts. Short-range electrostatic models (e.g., Damped Shifted Force) yield non-physical results at interfaces. Capping strategies are needed for resolution-related discontinuities. Bonded degree of freedom interpolation in the Hamiltonian is impossible.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides guidelines for correctly setting up H-AdResS simulations and helps researchers assess whether the method is suitable for their system.
